course.title: Cloud Fundamentals
course.description: The ideas behind every cloud provider, from regions and IAM to networks, storage, cost and recovery, with AWS as the worked example.
course.audience: A capable adult who has used web applications and knows basic computing and networking from CS basics. No cloud experience needed. Useful groundwork for the AWS Solutions Architect Associate, without being exam prep.

paragraphs: When a company rents computing from a cloud provider, it gets machines, storage and databases by sending requests to an interface, and it pays for them by the hour or by the gigabyte as it uses them. The machines are real, and they sit in data centres grouped into regions and zones that fail separately, while every request to use them is checked against policies that say who may do what. Those arrangements are much the same at every provider, and what changes from one to the next is mostly the names, so this course gives the idea first and then the AWS service that carries it, since AWS names are the ones most people meet.

Much of cloud design can be settled by arithmetic. The availability of a service follows from the availabilities of the parts it depends on, the size of a network follows from the length of its address prefix, a month's bill follows from quantities and prices, and the number of workers a queue needs follows from the rate at which messages arrive. Working these out lets you judge a design before it is built, including whether it survives the loss of a data centre and what it will cost to run. The prices quoted are illustrative and dated, and the same working applies to whatever a provider charges today.
That groundwork is also what the AWS Solutions Architect Associate certification expects, although the course is not written as exam preparation.
outcomes: You'll be able to place any task on the shared-responsibility line.
You'll be able to compute availability, address space, cost and queue sizing from stated numbers.
You'll be able to read an IAM-style policy and apply least privilege.
You'll be able to choose compute, storage and database types and map them to AWS names.
You'll be able to review a design against the six Well-Architected pillars and choose a recovery strategy.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, How Computers and Networks Work.

modules.title: The cloud model
modules.description: What the cloud is, where it physically sits, who is responsible for what, and who may do what.

modules.title: Building blocks
modules.description: Networks, compute, storage and databases, the pieces every design uses, with AWS names as the worked example.

modules.title: Designing for the cloud
modules.description: Scaling, decoupling, cost, the Well-Architected view, security and recovery.

concepts.title: Five characteristics
concepts.summary: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

concepts.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
concepts.summary: The three models differ by how much of the stack the provider runs for you.

concepts.title: Shared responsibility
concepts.summary: The provider secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what they put in it and how they configure it.

concepts.title: Region and availability zone
concepts.summary: A region is a geographic area; an availability zone is one or more discrete data centres within it, isolated for fault tolerance.

concepts.title: Availability
concepts.summary: The proportion of time a system is able to serve requests, often written as nines.

concepts.title: Redundancy
concepts.summary: Independent copies of a component, so one failure does not remove the function.

concepts.title: Principal and role
concepts.summary: A principal is an entity that can make requests; a role is an identity assumed temporarily, with short-lived credentials.

concepts.title: Policy
concepts.summary: A document that allows or denies actions on resources, optionally under conditions.

concepts.title: Policy evaluation
concepts.summary: Requests are denied by default; an explicit deny always overrides any allow.

concepts.title: CIDR block
concepts.summary: A prefix such as 10.0.0.0/16 whose length n leaves 2^(32-n) addresses.

concepts.title: Subnet and route table
concepts.summary: A subnet is a slice of the network in one zone; its route table decides where traffic goes.

concepts.title: Security group versus network ACL
concepts.summary: A security group is stateful and attached to a resource; a network ACL is stateless and attached to a subnet.

concepts.title: Virtual machine
concepts.summary: A rented slice of a server with its own operating system, billed by time.

concepts.title: Function as a service
concepts.summary: Code run per event, with no server to manage, billed by requests and duration.

concepts.title: Auto scaling
concepts.summary: A group that adds or removes instances according to a metric or schedule.

concepts.title: Object storage
concepts.summary: Whole objects addressed by key in a flat namespace, accessed over HTTP, with very high durability.

concepts.title: Block storage
concepts.summary: A raw disk attached to one machine, for operating systems and databases.

concepts.title: Durability versus availability
concepts.summary: Durability is the chance data is not lost; availability is the chance it can be read now.

concepts.title: RPO and RTO
concepts.summary: RPO is the most data, as time, you can afford to lose; RTO is the longest outage you can afford.

concepts.title: Multi-AZ versus read replica
concepts.summary: A multi-AZ standby is for failover; a read replica serves extra reads.

concepts.title: Relational, key-value and document
concepts.summary: The model is chosen by access patterns, consistency need and scale.

concepts.title: Load balancer
concepts.summary: Spreads requests across healthy targets and removes unhealthy ones.

concepts.title: Queue
concepts.summary: A buffer between producer and consumer that lets each run at its own pace.

concepts.title: Stateless tier
concepts.summary: A tier that keeps no per-user data locally, so any instance can serve any request.

concepts.title: Pay per use
concepts.summary: Charges track consumption, so cost is a function of design.

concepts.title: Data transfer out
concepts.summary: Data leaving the provider's network, or crossing regions, is charged per GB; data in is usually free.

concepts.title: Commitment pricing
concepts.summary: A lower rate in return for a promise of steady usage over a term.

concepts.title: Pillars
concepts.summary: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability.

concepts.title: Trade-off
concepts.summary: Strengthening one pillar usually costs another, so a design records what it chose.

concepts.title: Architecture review
concepts.summary: A structured set of questions that finds risks before they cause incidents.

concepts.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
concepts.summary: Data is encrypted on disk with managed keys, and on the wire with TLS.

concepts.title: Audit logging
concepts.summary: An append-only record of API calls, answering who did what, when and from where.

concepts.title: Accounts and guardrails
concepts.summary: Separate accounts limit blast radius; organisation-wide policies stop the worst actions.

concepts.title: Recovery strategies
concepts.summary: Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active/active, in rising cost and falling recovery time.

concepts.title: Three-tier design
concepts.summary: Load-balanced stateless web tier, application tier, and a replicated data tier across zones.

concepts.title: Failure testing
concepts.summary: Recovery that has not been rehearsed is only a hope.

lessons.title: What the cloud is

steps.headline: The cloud is defined by how computing is delivered, and the definition lists five characteristics.

lead.text: Hardware in a data centre is not what makes something a cloud, since a company can run a rack of servers in a cupboard and nobody would call it that. In September 2011 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published SP 800-145, a definition short enough to fit on two pages, and it describes the cloud by **five essential characteristics** of the way computing is delivered.

The first is **on-demand self-service**: you provision a server or a database yourself, through a console or an API, without waiting for a person at the provider to do it. **Broad network access** means the resources are reached over the network from ordinary clients, and **resource pooling** means the provider serves many customers from one large pool, assigning and reassigning parts of it as demand moves. The fourth, **rapid elasticity**, lets capacity grow and shrink quickly with demand, and the fifth, **measured service**, means that use is metered so that you pay for what you consumed.

afterFigure.text: Take any one away and the picture changes. Without self-service you are filing tickets, without elasticity you are buying for the busiest day of the year, and without metering a bill has nothing to follow. The five together are why "someone else's computer" is a poor description: the computer is the least interesting part.

diagram.alt: A table of the five essential characteristics of cloud computing, each name beside a short plain meaning.
diagram.caption: The five characteristics in the NIST definition.

steps.headline: The three service models differ in how much of the stack the provider runs for you.

lead.text: Every application rests on the same seven layers: the **facility** (building, power, cooling), the **hardware**, the **hypervisor** that divides one machine into virtual ones, the **operating system**, the **runtime** (the language and libraries your code needs), the **application** and the **data**. A service model is a choice about where, in that stack, the provider's work ends and yours begins.

In **infrastructure as a service** (IaaS) the provider runs the facility, the hardware and the hypervisor, and you receive a virtual machine, so the operating system and everything above it is yours. In **platform as a service** (PaaS) the provider also runs the operating system and the runtime, and you supply only the application and its data. In **software as a service** (SaaS) the provider runs the application as well, and what remains with you is the data and the settings that control who may use it.

afterFigure.text: The three are therefore not quality tiers, with SaaS as the premium one. They are three places to draw one line, and a team picks the place that gives it enough control without leaving it more upkeep than it can afford. In AWS terms, a virtual machine on EC2 is IaaS, an application deployed to Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS, and a hosted email or office product is SaaS. These are current illustrations; product names change faster than the idea does.

steps.headline: The provider secures the cloud itself, and the customer secures what is put in it and how it is configured.

lead.text: Providers describe the line between the two sides as the **shared responsibility model**. The provider is responsible for the security *of* the cloud: the buildings, the physical servers, the network between them and the software that divides them up. The customer is responsible for security *in* the cloud, which means their data, who may sign in, the firewall rules, and, depending on the service, the patching of what they run.

The line sits in a different place for each service, which is exactly the service-model idea applied to security. On an EC2 instance the guest operating system is yours to patch, since you rent a machine and the operating system inside it is part of what you run. On a managed database such as RDS the provider patches the operating system and the engine, but you still decide which networks and users may connect.

afterFigure.text: Two points are easy to lose. A managed service shrinks your list of duties without emptying it, and the duties that stay are those that depend on your own choices: data, access and configuration. A misconfigured setting in the customer's half is the customer's fault however carefully the provider has run its own.

steps.headline: Four tasks, placed on an EC2 instance, an IaaS service.

workedSteps.text: A disk in the server fails. Disks belong to the hardware layer, which the provider runs, so the provider replaces it.
You must set a firewall rule so that only port 443 is open to the internet. The rule is a setting on your instance, so it belongs to the customer.
The guest operating system needs a security patch. It is the layer you took on by choosing a virtual machine. Say who applies it.
The data you store on the instance's disk must be encrypted. You choose whether to turn it on and keep the keys, so the work is the customer's.

steps.headline: The same patch and access tasks, placed on RDS, a managed database.

workedSteps.text: The server needs an operating system patch. This is the first place the line has moved compared with EC2.
A new application wants to connect, so someone must decide which networks may reach the database. Say who decides.
The database holds customer records, and the settings that encrypt and protect them are yours to choose, so that duty stays with the customer.

steps.headline: NIST also names four deployment models, which describe who the cloud is for.

lead.text: The service models say how much of the stack you manage. The **deployment models** say who the cloud is shared with. A **public cloud** is open to the general public and run by a provider on its own premises, as AWS is. A **private cloud** is provisioned for one organisation, and may be owned and run by that organisation or by someone on its behalf. A **community cloud** is provisioned for a group of organisations with shared concerns, such as a set of hospitals with the same compliance duties. A **hybrid cloud** combines two or more of these that stay separate but are joined by technology that lets data and applications move between them.

Most of this course concerns the public cloud, because that is where the five characteristics are easiest to see and where the shared responsibility line is drawn most explicitly. The ideas carry over to the others with little change, since a private cloud that meets the NIST definition has the same characteristics and the same line, with the organisation taking the provider's side of it.

reveal.text: A team that needs to tune the operating system would step down to IaaS, and one that wants no application to maintain would step up to SaaS.
This is why a SaaS customer still has security work to do: sharing settings, sign-in and who can read stored mail are all choices of the customer.

lessons.orientation: The five characteristics of the cloud, the three service models, and where shared responsibility puts the line.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson explains regions and availability zones, and computes the availability of serial and redundant components.

blocks.text: In a traditional company, getting a new server meant raising a purchase request, waiting for approval, ordering the machine, and waiting again while it was delivered, racked and cabled, a sequence that often took weeks. Today the same server can be started by sending one request to a provider's interface, and it is usually running within a minute or two, and removed by another request when it is no longer needed.

The server itself is the same kind of machine in the same kind of building, and what has changed is the way it is delivered. That is why **the cloud** is defined by behaviour rather than by equipment: you obtain computing yourself when you need it and pay for what you use. Once a provider takes over the buying, racking and cabling, the useful question becomes which of the remaining duties, from patching an operating system to deciding who may read the data, it has also taken over and which are still yours.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the five essential characteristics and the three service models, and say whether the provider or the customer handles a given task.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later design choice in this course starts from the question of what you run and what the provider runs.

recap.keyIdea: The cloud is computing delivered with the five NIST characteristics, and each service model draws the line between provider and customer at a different layer.

blocks.text: The five characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service, and together they describe how the cloud is delivered. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are three places to draw one line through the same seven layers, and none of them is a better grade of the others.

Wherever the line falls, the provider secures the cloud itself while the customer secures what they put in it and how they configure it, so moving a workload to a managed service shortens your list of duties without removing data, access and configuration from it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at where the provider's machines are, and how to calculate how available a system built from them can be.

lessons.title: Regions, zones and availability

steps.headline: A region is a geographic area, and an availability zone is an isolated group of data centres inside it.

lead.text: A cloud provider's machines are not in one place. AWS groups them into **regions**, each a separate geographic area such as Northern Virginia or Frankfurt, and each region contains several **availability zones**. An availability zone is one or more discrete data centres with their own power, cooling and network connections, kept far enough apart that a fire, a flood or a power failure at one is unlikely to touch another, yet close enough for fast links between them.

That isolation is what makes a zone the useful unit for planning around failure. Inside a zone, failures are shared, since two servers there rely on the same building. Between zones they are largely independent, so a design that places copies in different zones is protected against losing any one of them. The figure shows one region with three zones, and its buttons show what survives when one zone fails and what survives when everything sits in one.

afterFigure.text: Notice what the database needs in the second view. A web server holds nothing worth keeping, so the other zones simply carry on with it, whereas a database holds the data, and so it keeps a **standby** copy in a second zone that takes over when the first is lost.

steps.headline: Availability is the share of time a system can serve requests, and each extra nine divides the downtime by ten.

lead.text: **Availability** is the proportion of time during which a system is able to serve requests, and it is usually quoted as a percentage. A year contains 525,600 minutes, so a system that is available 99.9% of the time may be unavailable for the other 0.1%, which is 525,600 × 0.001 = 525.6 minutes, or 8.76 hours. Reliability engineers speak of the *nines* in that figure: 99.9% is three nines, 99.99% is four.

The table shows the pattern. Each added nine leaves a tenth of the downtime allowed by the one before it, from 87.6 hours a year at 99% to about five minutes at 99.999%. Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* book makes the related point that a target above what users can perceive is wasted effort. The higher levels are also dearer, since each needs more redundancy and more operational discipline than the last, so the right target is the one the business needs and no more.

steps.headline: Components that are all required multiply their availabilities, so every extra one lowers the whole.

lead.text: Take two components that must both work, such as a web server and the database it reads from. If they fail independently, the chance that a given moment finds *both* working is the product of the two availabilities, which is 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.998001, or 99.8001%. Arranged this way the components are said to be **in series**, and the whole is always lower than its weakest part.

The loss looks small for two components and grows with each one added: three in series give 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.997003, or 99.7003%, which is 26.3 hours of downtime a year rather than 8.76. A real request often passes through a load balancer, a web server, a cache and a database, and so the availability users see is the product of all of them, which is why adding a dependency is never free.

afterFigure.text: The multiplication holds only when failures are independent, and that is also the condition that decides when redundancy helps, which is the next idea.

Multiply them.
Give the product as a percentage. Work out the figure.

steps.headline: Independent copies in parallel fail only when all of them fail at once, which raises availability.

lead.text: Redundancy runs the other way. Place two copies of a component side by side, so that either can serve the request, and the pair fails only at the moments when *both* are down. For independent copies that chance is the product of the two failure chances: each is down 0.001 of the time, so both are down 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.000001 of the time, and the pair is available 1 − 0.000001 = 0.999999, or 99.9999%. Two components of three nines become one of six, and the figure compares the pair with a single copy.

The word *independent* carries the whole result. Two servers in the same zone share a building, a power feed and a network switch, so a single event can take both, and the product of their failure chances understates how often the pair fails. Servers in different availability zones are as close to independent as an ordinary design can make them, which is why zones, rather than extra servers in one place, are how redundancy is bought.

steps.headline: Latency, data rules and price decide which region to use, and zones decide how to survive failure.

lead.text: Two separate questions are easily confused. *Which region* is a question about where the work belongs, and AWS's guidance lists the usual reasons: how close the region is to your users, since distance adds delay; where the law or your contracts allow the data to live, which is called **data residency**; which services the region offers; and what they cost there. *Which zones* is a question about surviving failure, and it is answered by spreading the design across at least two of them.

A region is also a wide boundary. Copying a design to a second region protects against the loss of an entire region and is considerably dearer, since the regions are far apart and data has to cross between them, so it is a choice made for a stated recovery need and not by default. The same reasoning applies to the nines: each extra one is a purchase with a cost, and it needs a reason.

reveal.text: The balancer limits the total, so a second balancer would help more than a third web server.

lessons.orientation: Regions and availability zones, availability expressed in nines, and the series and parallel rules.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson sets out who and what may act on cloud resources, using IAM-style policies and least privilege.

blocks.text: A system that is available 99.9% of the time may be down for 525.6 minutes a year, which is 8.76 hours, and one at 99.99% may be down for 52.56 minutes. The extra nine sounds like a rounding detail, yet it is a ten-fold difference in downtime, and it decides how a service has to be built.

A single server in a single building cannot reach four nines, because the building itself fails now and then through a fire, a flood or a power failure. Providers therefore divide their capacity into availability zones that fail separately, and the availability of a design built across them can be worked out from the availabilities of its parts, so you can tell before anything is built how many nines a design will deliver and what each extra one will cost.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate the availability of components in series and in parallel, and place servers so that one lost zone does not take the service down.
intro.whyItMatters: Availability figures decide how much redundancy a design needs and what it will cost.

recap.keyIdea: Availability multiplies for required components in series and rises for independent copies in parallel, so a design survives a failure by placing copies in separate availability zones.

blocks.text: Availability is the share of time a system can serve requests, quoted in nines, and each added nine divides the allowed downtime by ten. Components that are all required multiply their availabilities, which lowers the whole, while independent copies fail together only when each fails, which raises it.

A region is a geographic area and a zone is an isolated group of data centres inside it, so copies placed in separate zones fail close to independently. That is the reason designs span zones, and the reason each extra nine has to be justified.

lessons.title: Identity and access management

steps.headline: Every request names a principal, an action and a resource, and a policy decides whether it is permitted.

lead.text: When you click a button in the AWS console, or run a command, the request that reaches the service carries three facts: who is asking, what they want to do, and to which thing. The asker is a **principal**, an entity that can make requests, such as a person's user, an application, or a role. The wish is an **action**, written as a service name and an operation, for example s3:GetObject to read a file from S3. The thing is a **resource**, such as one bucket or one object in it.

Identity and access management, **IAM**, is the part of AWS that decides whether such a request is permitted, and it does so by reading **policies**: documents that allow or deny actions on resources, optionally under conditions. The policies attached to the principal, together with those attached to the resource, make up the whole of what IAM knows. Everything else in this lesson is the order in which it reads them.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the full order of checks that settles this.

steps.headline: IAM denies by default, an allow can open a request, and an explicit deny overrides every allow.

lead.text: IAM evaluates a request in a fixed order. It first looks for an **explicit deny**, a statement that names the action and resource with Deny, and if it finds one the request is denied at once. If there is none, it looks for a statement that allows the action on the resource, and if it finds one the request is allowed. If it finds neither, the request is denied, which is called **default deny**.

The three views in the figure follow three requests through that order. A matching allow with no deny gives *allowed*. The same kind of request, aimed at an object a second policy explicitly denies, is denied however many allows exist, because the deny is found first. A request nothing mentions is denied by default, and that is why a new user with no policies can do nothing at all.

afterFigure.text: The asymmetry is the design. Because an explicit deny wins everywhere, an administrator can place a deny that no later allow can undo, and because the default is deny, a mistake of omission is safe where a mistake of commission is not.

diagram.alt: A decision flow for a request. First it checks for an explicit deny, then for a matching allow, and otherwise it is denied by default. Three views show an allow only, an allow with a deny, and a request nothing mentions.
diagram.caption: Every request passes the same three checks in the same order. Use the buttons to follow three requests.

steps.headline: A policy statement has an effect, an action, a resource and optionally a condition.

lead.text: Policies are written in JSON, and each one holds a list of **statements**. A statement has an Effect, which is Allow or Deny; an Action, naming what may be done; a Resource, naming what it is done to; and optionally a Condition, which makes the statement apply only when something is true. The * character matches any run of characters, so arn:aws:s3:::reports/* stands for every object in the bucket called reports. An *ARN*, or Amazon Resource Name, is simply the full unique name of a resource.

Read the statement in the figure as a sentence: allow reading an object from any place in the reports bucket, but only when the caller signed in with multi-factor authentication. The condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is one AWS provides, and a condition can also limit a statement by network address, by time or by tag. A statement without a condition applies every time its action and resource match.

steps.headline: Evaluate a request against a policy that allows only s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::reports/*.

workedSteps.text: The request is s3:PutObject on reports/q1.csv. First look for an explicit deny; the policy contains none.
Next look for an allow that names this action. The only allow names s3:GetObject, which is a different action, so no allow matches.
With neither a deny nor an allow, the default applies. Say what the decision is.

steps.headline: Roles give services short-lived credentials, and the root user is kept for the few jobs that need it.

lead.text: Policies attach to identities, and the identity worth understanding best is the **role**. A role has no password and no permanent keys; a principal *assumes* it and receives credentials that expire, an hour later by default for a call to assume a role. A server can be given a role directly, so its code never carries a stored secret, and a stolen set of expired credentials is of no use. A long-lived access key written into a configuration file is the opposite case: it works until someone notices and deletes it.

Every account also has a **root user**, the identity created with the account, which can do everything and cannot be restricted by ordinary policies. AWS advises using it only for the handful of tasks that need it, protecting it with multi-factor authentication, and doing daily work as other identities with policies of their own.

steps.headline: Evaluate a delete request when one policy allows all S3 actions on reports/* and another denies s3:DeleteObject on reports/*.

workedSteps.text: The request is s3:DeleteObject on reports/q1.csv. The evaluation looks for an explicit deny first.
The second policy denies exactly this action on exactly this resource, so an explicit deny matches.
The first policy's allow would have matched, but it is never reached. Give the decision.

steps.headline: Least privilege grants only the actions and resources a task needs, and widens only when a need is shown.

lead.text: The practical rule that follows is **least privilege**: give each principal the actions and resources its task requires and nothing more. A policy that allows s3:* on every bucket works, which is its danger, since a leaked credential or a bug can then do anything to any bucket. A policy that allows s3:GetObject on one prefix lets the nightly job do its work and limits what a mistake can reach.

Starting narrow is easier than tightening later. Begin with the smallest policy that works, widen it when a request fails for a reason you accept, and use a condition, such as requiring multi-factor authentication or a source network, where one fits. Each unneeded permission is a quantity you can count, as in a policy with 10 actions across 3 buckets, which grants 30 action-and-resource pairs where two actions would grant 6.

reveal.text: Reading the job's requirements first is the habit to take away, since the policy then follows from them.
The count is a rough measure, but it shows why widening a policy has a real cost.

lessons.orientation: How IAM decides a request: principals, policies, default deny, explicit deny, roles and least privilege.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson builds virtual networks: sizing CIDR blocks, carving subnets and deciding what makes a subnet public.

blocks.text: A small policy in AWS looks like this: Effect Allow, Action s3:GetObject, Resource arn:aws:s3:::reports/*, in a JSON document whose Version field is the date 2012-10-17. Three short lines decide whether a program may read files from one bucket, and the same structure governs thousands of other actions across the platform.

Every request in AWS, from a click in the console to a call from a running program, is checked against policies like this one before anything happens. The check reads the policies in a fixed order, and knowing that order lets you say in advance whether any request will succeed, which matters because a policy that grants too much works perfectly well until a leaked key or a bug makes use of what it allows.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out whether a request is allowed under a set of policies, and say what least privilege asks you to change.
intro.whyItMatters: Misconfigured access is the commonest way cloud data is exposed, and you now own that side of the line.

recap.keyIdea: IAM denies a request unless a policy allows it, an explicit deny overrides every allow, and each principal should hold only what its task needs.

blocks.text: A request names a principal, an action and a resource, and IAM checks it for an explicit deny, then for an allow, and denies it if it finds neither. Policies say what is allowed or denied in statements of effect, action, resource and condition, and roles give services credentials that expire instead of keys that last.

Least privilege applies the same machinery with discipline: start with the smallest policy that does the job and widen it only when a real need appears. The root user is kept away from daily work, since it is the one identity policies cannot restrain.

lessons.title: Virtual networks

steps.headline: A prefix such as /16 fixes the first bits of an address, and the bits left free set how many addresses the block holds.

lead.text: Every address in a virtual network is a 32-bit number, written as four numbers from 0 to 255. A **CIDR block** names a range of such addresses by giving one address and a **prefix length**: in 10.0.0.0/16, the 16 says that the first 16 bits are fixed and the remaining 16 are free to vary. Every address in the block begins 10.0, and the last two numbers can be anything.

That makes the arithmetic short. A block with prefix length n leaves 32 − n free bits, and so holds 2^(32−n) addresses: a /16 holds 2^16 = 65,536, a /24 holds 2^8 = 256 and a /28 holds 2^4 = 16. Each bit added to the prefix halves the block. CIDR, which stands for classless inter-domain routing, was introduced in 1993 to slow the growth of routing tables and the exhaustion of addresses, and RFC 4632, published in 2006, is its current description.

afterFigure.text: A **virtual private cloud**, or VPC, is your own private network inside a provider's, and you give it a CIDR block when you create it. AWS accepts IPv4 blocks of sizes from /16 down to /28.

reveal.text: Four more free bits than a /24 gives 16 times as many addresses.

steps.headline: Is 10.0.2.5 inside the block 10.0.1.0/24?

workedSteps.text: A /24 fixes the first 24 bits, which are the first three numbers of the address.
The address 10.0.2.5 begins 10.0.2, and the block requires 10.0.1. Compare the two.
The third number differs, so the address is in a different block. Say whether it is inside.

steps.headline: A subnet is a slice of the network inside one zone, and its route table decides where its traffic goes.

lead.text: You divide the network into **subnets**, each a smaller CIDR block that lives in exactly one availability zone. A /16 divides into 256 subnets of /24, since 2^(24−16) = 2^8 = 256, and a design that places one subnet in each of two or three zones can put copies of a service in each, in the way the availability lesson required.

Each subnet is tied to a **route table**, a list of rules saying where traffic for a given destination goes. A route for the network's own range stays inside it, and any other destination needs a route of its own. AWS keeps 5 addresses in every subnet for itself: the first address names the network, the next three go to the router, the DNS service and a spare, and the last is a broadcast address, so a /24 offers 251 usable addresses and a /27 offers 27.

reveal.text: A /28 is the smallest block AWS allows, and it leaves fewer than three quarters of its addresses.
The next screen explains what the route table does.

steps.headline: A subnet is public when its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway, and a NAT gateway gives private subnets outbound access.

lead.text: A subnet's name does not make it public. It is public when two things are true: its route table has a route sending internet traffic to an **internet gateway**, the VPC's door to the internet, and its resources have public addresses. The route is written as the destination 0.0.0.0/0, a prefix of length 0 that matches every address, so it catches any traffic that no more specific route claims. Take the route away and the same subnet is private, as the first view shows.

Private servers still often need to call out, to download updates or reach an external service. A **NAT gateway**, which sits in a public subnet, lets them do so: their route table sends internet traffic to it, and it forwards the requests with its own public address and brings the replies back. Nothing outside can start a connection to them, which is why databases and application servers usually live in private subnets.

workedSteps.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC. The gateway is the door; nothing uses it yet.
Give the subnet's route table a route that sends all other traffic to the gateway. Name the destination of that default route.

Give the servers public addresses, and open the ports they serve in their security group, the filter attached to each server that the last part of this lesson explains. Without these, the route exists but nothing answers.

steps.headline: A security group is stateful and attached to a resource, and a network ACL is stateless and attached to a subnet.

lead.text: Two filters limit traffic. A **security group** is attached to a resource, such as a server, and is **stateful**: it remembers each connection it let in, so the replies go out without any rule of their own. It holds allow rules only, and everything not allowed is blocked. A **network ACL** is attached to a whole subnet and is **stateless**: it judges every packet alone, so a reply needs its own rule, and it can both allow and deny, checking its numbered rules from the lowest number up and acting on the first match.

Most designs lean on security groups, which are simpler and sit closest to the resource, and keep the default network ACL, which allows all traffic. A network ACL is the tool for a blunt rule across a subnet, such as blocking one hostile address range, and its statelessness is the common reason a setup that looks right does not work.

blocks.text: A network block written 10.0.0.0/16 holds 2^16 = 65,536 addresses, while 10.0.1.0/24 holds only 256, and a single bit added to the prefix is enough to halve the size. Anyone who builds a network in the cloud has to choose these sizes in advance, because a block cannot easily be resized once servers are using it.

Inside such a block you divide the addresses into subnets, give each subnet a route table that says where its traffic may go, and place filters in front of the servers. Those choices decide, before any server starts, which machines the internet can reach and which can be reached only from inside the network, so a network laid out with care can keep a database out of public view while the web servers in front of it answer requests from anywhere.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the addresses in a CIDR block, carve it into subnets, and say what makes a subnet public.
intro.whyItMatters: Address blocks are hard to change later, and one misrouted subnet can expose a database.

recap.keyIdea: A prefix of length n leaves 2^(32−n) addresses, and a subnet is public only when its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway.

blocks.text: A CIDR block with prefix length n holds 2^(32−n) addresses, so each extra bit in the prefix halves it, and a /16 divides into 256 subnets of /24. On AWS five addresses in every subnet are reserved, which leaves 251 usable in a /24.

Public and private are properties of the route table: a subnet is public when its route sends internet traffic to an internet gateway and its resources have public addresses, and private servers reach out through a NAT gateway. Security groups are stateful and attach to resources, while network ACLs are stateless and attach to subnets.

lessons.title: Compute: machines, containers and functions

steps.headline: Virtual machines, containers and functions trade control against the effort of running them.

lead.text: Compute is the part of a system that runs your code, and the cloud offers it at three levels. A **virtual machine** is a rented slice of a physical server with its own operating system, which you configure and patch, and it is billed by the time it exists. A **container** packages an application with everything it needs, so it runs the same wherever it is placed, and a container service runs many of them on shared machines. A **function** is a piece of code the provider runs for you when an event arrives, with no machine to manage, billed by requests and running time.

Moving along that list gives up control to remove work: the machine lets you install anything, the container asks you to package one application, and the function asks you only for the code. A function also comes with limits, among them a cap of 15 minutes for each run in AWS, so some work does not fit it. The figure rates the three options for four workloads, and the reasons matter more than the marks.

steps.headline: Virtual machines come in families that differ in the ratio of CPU, memory and network, and they are billed by the hour.

lead.text: A provider offers machines in **instance types** grouped into families, each family weighted towards one resource: some give more memory for each CPU, some more CPUs, some faster networking. Choosing a type is choosing a ratio to suit the workload, such as a database that needs memory or a video encoder that needs processors, and a machine can be changed to a larger or smaller type if the first guess was wrong.

Billing follows the clock. Using an illustrative price of $0.10 an hour, which is not a quote and dated November 2026, one instance running for a month of about 730 hours costs 0.10 × 730 = $73.00, and a pair costs 2 × 73.00 = $146.00. Providers also sell a **commitment discount**, a lower rate in exchange for a promise to use a certain amount for one or three years, and an illustrative discount of 40% would bring the $146.00 down to $87.60.

steps.headline: Three instances at $0.10 an hour for a month of 730 hours.

workedSteps.text: One instance costs its hourly price times the hours in the month.
The group has three, so multiply by three. Work out the monthly cost.

steps.headline: Apply a 40% commitment discount to the same group.

workedSteps.text: A 40% discount removes 40% of the price, which leaves 60%.
The discounted price is 60% of $219.00, which is 0.6 × 219. Work it out.

steps.headline: An auto scaling group adds and removes instances to follow demand, between a minimum and a maximum.

lead.text: Capacity bought for the busiest hour sits idle the rest of the day, so the cloud lets a group of identical instances change size automatically. An **auto scaling group** is given a **minimum**, a **maximum** and a rule, such as keeping average CPU use near 50%. When the metric rises the group launches instances, when it falls it ends them, and it never goes below the minimum or above the maximum. Placing the group's instances across zones is the point to keep in mind, since a group whose instances all sit in one zone shares the fate of that zone.

The minimum protects availability, because it keeps enough instances running to carry the load if one fails. The maximum protects the bill, because a fault that makes demand look endless would otherwise buy capacity without limit. More instances therefore do not by themselves mean more resilience; instances in separate zones do.

reveal.text: The next screen describes how a function is run and billed.

steps.headline: A function runs per event, is billed by requests and running time, and can be cheaper or dearer than a machine.

lead.text: Functions give up the always-running machine altogether. The provider starts your code when an event arrives, such as a web request or a new file, runs it, and bills for the **requests** and for the **running time**, counted in GB-seconds, which is the memory the function is given multiplied by the seconds it runs. Servers still exist, run by the provider, so *serverless* means that you do not manage them. The first request after a quiet period may wait while the provider prepares an environment, a delay called a **cold start**.

Take illustrative prices, dated November 2026: $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000167 per GB-second. A function with 0.5 GB of memory that runs for 0.2 seconds uses 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1 GB-seconds a call, so a million calls cost $0.20 for requests and 1,000,000 × 0.1 × 0.0000167 = $1.67 for running time, $1.87 in all. A single machine at $73.00 a month costs the same at about 39 million calls. Below that the function is cheaper, and above it, if one machine can serve the load, the machine is.

afterFigure.text: The figure plots both costs. A function is therefore not always the cheaper choice; at a steady, high load a machine can cost less, and a commitment discount moves the crossing point lower still.

lessons.orientation: Virtual machines, containers and functions compared by control and cost, with auto scaling and illustrative prices.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson compares object, block and file storage and explains durability figures.

blocks.text: Two instances billed at an illustrative $0.10 an hour for 730 hours cost 2 × 0.10 × 730 = $146.00 a month, and a commitment discount of 40% brings that to $87.60. A function that handles 5 million requests, on the other hand, costs $1.00 in request charges and nothing at all while it waits for the next one.

Both are ways of renting compute, and they differ in what you pay for and in what you have to manage yourself. A machine is billed for every hour it runs, busy or idle, while a function is billed only for the requests it serves and the time it spends on them, so which is cheaper depends on the load, and from the prices alone you can find the number of requests a month at which the two cost the same. The prices here are illustrative and dated November 2026, and the same working applies to whatever a provider charges today.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between virtual machines, containers and functions for a workload, and work out what each would cost from stated prices.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong compute model is the commonest way to pay too much or to build something that needs constant care.

recap.keyIdea: Virtual machines, containers and functions trade control for effort, and which is cheaper depends on how steady and how large the load is.

blocks.text: A virtual machine gives full control and is billed by the hour, a container packages one application for shared machines, and a function runs per event and is billed by requests and running time. Auto scaling keeps the number of instances between a minimum and a maximum, and instances spread across zones are what give resilience.

Serverless still has servers, run by the provider. Costs follow from the prices: an hourly price times 730 hours for a machine, and a per-million charge plus GB-seconds for a function, so the cheaper option changes where the two lines cross.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to storage, and the three kinds of it that compute attaches to.

lessons.title: Storage: object, block and file

steps.headline: Object, block and file storage differ in how data is addressed and who can use it.

lead.text: Storage is chosen by the way it is accessed. **Object storage** holds whole items, called objects, in a flat space of buckets and is reached over HTTP by a name called a key; Amazon S3 is the standard example. **Block storage** is a raw disk, a series of numbered blocks, which one machine formats and uses as its own; Amazon EBS is the AWS form. **File storage** is a shared folder that many machines mount over the network and open as ordinary files; Amazon EFS is the AWS form.

The three are not grades of one product, since each fits a pattern the others handle badly. A database engine wants a block volume, because it changes small pieces of a disk constantly. A fleet of web servers that must see the same uploaded files wants a file system. Backups, images and logs, which are written once and read whole, belong in object storage, which is also the cheapest of the three per gigabyte.

diagram.alt: Three kinds of storage side by side: object storage holds whole objects by key in a bucket, block storage is a raw disk attached to one machine, and file storage is a shared folder many servers mount.

steps.headline: An object store has no real directory tree, and it keeps versions and moves data between classes by rule.

lead.text: An object store looks like a file system but is not one. A key such as reports/2026/q3.csv is a single name; the slashes are only characters, and the console shows a *prefix* such as reports/ as if it were a folder. There is no partial edit either, since changing one byte means uploading the whole object again, and a rename is a copy followed by a delete.

Two features make up for that. **Versioning** keeps every earlier version of an object when it is overwritten or deleted, so a mistake can be undone. **Lifecycle rules** act on objects by age, for example moving them to a cheaper class after 30 days or deleting them after a year. Both are settings the customer chooses, in keeping with the shared responsibility line from the first lesson.

reveal.text: The next screen names the two measures and the numbers quoted for each.

steps.headline: Durability is the chance data is not lost, and availability is the chance it can be read now.

lead.text: **Durability** is the probability that data is not lost over a period, and **availability**, met in the second lesson, is the probability that it can be read at a given moment. They are separate: a storage service can be briefly out of reach and lose nothing, and the figure shows that case beside a real loss. S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability, written *eleven nines*, together with a design target of 99.99% availability.

Eleven nines means an annual chance of loss of 10^−11 for each object. Multiplying by the number of objects gives the expected loss: for 1,000,000 objects that is 10^6 × 10^−11 = 10^−5 = 0.00001 objects a year, about one object in 100,000 years. The figure is a design target built on keeping copies in several zones, and it covers failures of the hardware. It does not cover a deletion that you make yourself.

steps.headline: Expected loss for 10,000,000 objects at an annual chance of 10^-11 each.

workedSteps.text: The expected number of losses is the number of objects times the chance for each. Write 10,000,000 as a power of ten.
Multiply, adding the exponents.
Write the answer as a decimal number of objects a year.

steps.headline: The same calculation for 1,000,000,000 objects.

workedSteps.text: A billion is 10^9, a hundred times as many objects as before.
Multiply by the same chance of 10^-11, adding the exponents. Work out the expected loss per year as a decimal.

steps.headline: Storage classes trade the price of holding data against the speed and cost of reading it.

lead.text: S3 offers **storage classes** for data of different ages. The standard class is built for data that is read often. Colder classes cost less to hold but add a delay or a fee when the data is read, and the coldest, the archive classes, can take hours to return an object. The table gives illustrative prices from November 2026, per gigabyte per month: $0.023 for standard, $0.0125 for infrequent access, $0.0036 for a flexible archive and $0.00099 for a deep archive.

A lifecycle rule moves data down this list as it ages, and the saving is real only when data is read rarely. Holding 10,000 GB costs 10,000 × 0.023 = $230.00 in the standard class, and 10,000 × 0.0125 = $125.00 in infrequent access, which is a saving of $105.00 until the retrieval fee for data that is read back is added.

steps.headline: Replication copies data faithfully, mistakes included, so it does not replace versioned backups.

lead.text: Copies in several places protect against hardware failure and they do not protect against yourself. A replica of a bucket receives the same writes as the original, so a bad overwrite, a corrupted file or a deletion travels to the copy as faithfully as good data does, and the copy is then equally wrong. A backup is different in one way that matters: it keeps an earlier state that later changes cannot reach.

The working rule is to combine the features. Versioning keeps earlier versions of objects, snapshots keep earlier states of a block volume, and a restore is tested from time to time, since a backup that has never been restored is only a hope. Durability figures describe the provider's side of the shared responsibility line, and recovery from your own mistakes is on yours.

reveal.text: A tested restore from versions would have returned the folder, which is why backups are tested and not merely taken.

lessons.orientation: Object, block and file storage, durability figures and the difference between replication and backup.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson chooses a database model, separates multi-AZ from read replicas, and applies RPO and RTO.

blocks.text: Amazon S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability, a figure with eleven nines. Spelled out, it is an annual chance of 10^−11 that any one object is lost, so someone who stores 1,000,000 objects can expect to lose one about every 100,000 years. The number is easy to misread, since it describes the chance that the provider loses an object and says nothing about a file that its owner deleted by mistake.

S3 is object storage, one of three kinds that cloud providers offer, and the three differ in how a program reaches the data, which decides the work each one suits. Their durability and availability figures differ too, and reading those figures correctly is how you tell which failures a design is already protected against and which still have to be guarded by other means.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to match a need to object, block or file storage, and interpret a durability figure as an expected loss.
intro.whyItMatters: Picking storage by access pattern decides cost and design, and misreading durability leads to data that has no real backup.

recap.keyIdea: Object, block and file storage suit different access patterns, and durability is the chance data is lost, which is not the same as availability or a backup.

blocks.text: Object storage holds whole objects by key over HTTP, block storage is a raw disk for one machine, and file storage is a shared folder for many. Durability is the chance data is not lost and availability is the chance it can be read now, and eleven nines of durability means an expected loss of 0.0001 objects a year among 10,000,000.

Storage classes trade holding costs against reading costs, so they save money only for data that is read rarely. Replication protects against hardware failure but copies mistakes as faithfully as data, so versioned backups and tested restores remain the customer's work.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves on to databases, and to how much data and time a failure may be allowed to cost.

lessons.title: Databases and recovery objectives

steps.headline: A managed database takes on the server work, and the customer still owns the schema, the queries, the access and the size.

lead.text: A database run by the provider, such as Amazon RDS, removes the work of installing the engine, patching the server and operating system, and keeping backups running, which is the provider's side of the line described in the first lesson. It leaves the rest with you: the design of the tables, the quality of the queries, who may connect, and how large the instance is, since a database sized too small is slow and one sized too large is costly.

The first misconception to drop is that *managed* means *no administration*. The provider can keep a server healthy, but it cannot tell that a query scans a hundred million rows when it needs ten, or that an access rule is too wide. The remaining work is smaller and more interesting, and it starts with picking a data model.

steps.headline: The right database model follows the access pattern, the consistency needed and the scale.

lead.text: A **relational** database stores tables of rows linked by keys, and answers questions that join them with SQL; it also provides transactions, so several changes succeed or fail together, which is why it is the usual home of orders, accounts and payments. A **key-value** store keeps items that are fetched by a key and nothing else, which lets it hold steady speed at very large scale, at the price of having no joins. A **document** database keeps nested JSON-like documents, each holding a whole record, and suits records whose fields differ from one to the next.

No model is better in general. The decision is made from the questions the application asks: if it asks across related data, choose relational; if it asks for one item by identity millions of times a second, choose key-value; if each record is a self-contained document that varies in shape, choose a document store. The figure sets the three side by side with the AWS service that provides each.

diagram.alt: Three database models compared by data shape, best use, an AWS example and the main trade-off: relational, key-value and document.

steps.headline: RPO limits the data you can lose and RTO limits how long you can be down.

lead.text: Two numbers describe a recovery requirement. The **recovery point objective**, or **RPO**, is the most data, measured as time, that you can afford to lose. The **recovery time objective**, or **RTO**, is the longest outage you can afford. They are set by the business and then met by the design, in that order: a payments service may need an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes, and a reporting database may be content with a day of each.

Backups set the RPO. If backups run every 6 hours, a failure just before the next one loses up to 6 hours of changes, and a backup taken at midnight does not give an RPO of nothing. The figure marks the last backup before a failure and shades the changes made since, which are the data lost. The RTO is measured from the moment of failure to the moment service is restored, and it includes the time to notice the failure, to restore and to switch traffic over.

afterFigure.text: Each number can be met, at a price, but not both for free: a smaller RPO needs more frequent copies, and a smaller RTO needs a standby that is already running.

steps.headline: A multi-AZ standby exists to take over, and a read replica exists to serve more reads.

lead.text: These two features are often confused, because each is a second copy of the database. A **multi-AZ standby** sits in another availability zone and is kept in step **synchronously**, so each committed change reaches it before the write is confirmed. It cannot be queried while the primary is healthy; its job is to take over, which AWS does automatically, usually within a couple of minutes, with no committed data lost. A **read replica** is fed **asynchronously**, so it trails the primary by a **replication lag** of a moment or more, and its job is to take read queries off the primary.

The consequences follow from that. A replica can serve stale data, so it suits reports and pages that tolerate it, and it does not give high availability by itself, though one can be promoted by hand. A standby gives failover but adds no read capacity. A design that needs both has both, in different zones, as the figure shows.

diagram.alt: A database primary in zone a with a standby in zone b kept in step synchronously, and a read replica in zone c fed asynchronously. A second view shows the primary failing and the standby taking over.
diagram.caption: The standby exists for failover and the replica exists for extra reads. Use the buttons to fail the primary.

reveal.text: Adding a standby would have cost the same and fixed nothing, which is the usual result of mixing the two up.

steps.headline: Automated backups and point-in-time recovery set the RPO, and only a tested restore proves it.

lead.text: Managed databases take automated backups and store the transaction log between them, which makes **point-in-time recovery** possible: a restore to any moment within a retention window, set by you at up to 35 days in RDS, with an RPO of a few minutes and not the backup interval. The restore creates a new database, so there is work to switch over to it, and that work belongs to the RTO.

A backup that has never been restored is an assumption. Practise the restore, time it, and compare the time with the RTO, because the time taken to detect the fault and to repoint the application is usually larger than the restore itself, as the next question shows.

reveal.text: Each stage can be shortened separately, and detection is often the cheapest to improve.

lessons.orientation: Choosing a database model, multi-AZ versus read replica, and applying RPO and RTO.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson sizes worker pools from arrival and service rates and uses queues and load balancers to remove coupling.

blocks.text: A database that fails at 10:00 and is serving again at 10:45 has been out for 45 minutes, and if the business had said it could tolerate 30, the recovery missed its target by 15 minutes. Some data may be gone as well, namely every change made since the last copy that survived the failure.

Those two quantities, how long a recovery may take and how much recent data it may lose, are the measurements that recovery planning is built on, and the business sets them by deciding what it can bear. They come before any choice of technology, because once they are stated you can check whether a backup schedule, a standby copy or a restore plan actually meets them, and so judge which of a managed database's features are worth paying for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to match a workload to a database model, tell a multi-AZ standby from a read replica, and work out RPO and RTO from a timeline.
intro.whyItMatters: RPO and RTO turn a vague wish to be safe into numbers a design can be checked against.

recap.keyIdea: Backups set the RPO and recovery speed sets the RTO, and a multi-AZ standby handles failover while a read replica handles extra reads.

blocks.text: A managed database takes on servers and patching, and leaves the schema, queries, access and sizing with you. The model is chosen by the access pattern: relational for questions across related data, key-value for huge numbers of lookups by key, and document for records that vary in shape.

RPO is the data you can lose and RTO is the outage you can bear, and backups every 6 hours give a worst-case RPO of 6 hours. A multi-AZ standby is for failover and a read replica is for reads with some lag, so neither stands in for the other.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how to add capacity as demand grows, and at how queues and load balancers keep parts of a system from depending on each other.

lessons.title: Scaling and decoupling

steps.headline: Scaling up grows one machine, and scaling out adds machines, and only the second has no ceiling.

lead.text: A service that has outgrown its server can be helped in two ways. **Scaling up**, also called vertical scaling, moves to a larger machine, with more CPU and memory. It is simple, because nothing in the design changes, but it has a ceiling, which is the largest machine on offer, and it leaves one machine as a single point of failure. **Scaling out**, or horizontal scaling, adds more machines of the same size and shares the work among them.

Scaling out removes both limits, since there is no largest fleet and a failure costs only the share of work that machine carried. It requires a design that lets one machine be swapped for another, and the next idea, keeping the tier stateless, is what allows that.

diagram.alt: Two ways to add capacity. Scaling up replaces one machine with a larger one, which has a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Scaling out adds more machines behind a load balancer.

reveal.text: Replacing a machine by a larger one usually needs a restart, a further reason to prefer adding machines.

steps.headline: A load balancer spreads requests across healthy servers, and it works best when no server keeps per-user data.

lead.text: A **load balancer** receives every request and forwards it to one of several servers, and it sends a periodic **health check** to each server so that one that stops answering is removed from rotation until it recovers. AWS's Elastic Load Balancing does this across servers in more than one availability zone, which connects it with the lesson on zones: the balancer itself is spread out, and servers in several zones keep serving when one zone is lost.

A balancer is only useful if any server can handle any request. A tier with that property is **stateless**, meaning that it keeps no per-user data of its own between requests. If a login session lives in one server's memory, the user is tied to that server and loses the session when it fails, as the first view shows. Moving the session to a shared store, as the second view shows, makes the servers interchangeable, and so makes it safe to add and remove them.

diagram.alt: A user's requests pass through a load balancer to servers. In the first view the session lives in one server's memory, tying the user to it. In the second the session lives in a shared store and either server can serve any request.

reveal.text: The next screen describes the queue that holds the backlog, and then the chart plots it.

steps.headline: A queue lets a producer and a consumer run at their own pace, so one can fail or slow without stopping the other.

lead.text: Coupling means that one part cannot work unless another is working at the same time. A **queue** removes it: a producer puts a message in the queue and carries on, and a consumer takes messages out when it is ready. AWS's Simple Queue Service, SQS, is the usual form. If the consumer is slow, restarting or gone, the messages wait in the queue instead of being lost, and a burst of arrivals is absorbed instead of overwhelming the consumers.

The queue does not make work disappear. Its contents are a **backlog**, the messages waiting to be processed, and it holds only as long as consumers eventually catch up. If messages arrive faster than the workers can process them, the backlog grows, and a queue with no limit simply moves the failure from the moment a request arrives to some later time.

diagram.alt: Producers send messages into a queue and consumers take them out. Three views: normal flow, one consumer lost with messages waiting, and a burst of messages that the queue absorbs.

steps.headline: The number of workers needed is the arrival rate divided by the rate of one worker, rounded up.

lead.text: The rule for sizing a pool follows from comparing two rates. If messages arrive at 120 a second and one worker handles 50 a second, the pool must handle at least 120 a second, so it needs 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4 workers. Since workers come whole, it needs **3**, and the fraction is always rounded up. With 2 workers the capacity is 100 a second, which is 20 short, and the backlog gains 20 messages each second, or 20 × 300 = 6,000 in five minutes.

The chart plots that for one, two and three workers. With one the backlog climbs fastest, with two it still climbs, and with three the capacity of 150 a second exceeds the arrivals and the queue stays empty. That leaves 30 messages a second spare, which is a sensible margin, since a pool run at exactly its limit has no room for a bad moment.

diagram.alt: A chart of queue depth over five minutes with 120 messages arriving each second and workers that each handle 50 a second. With one worker the depth reaches 21,000, with two it reaches 6,000, and with three it stays at zero.
diagram.caption: Depth rises while arrivals exceed capacity. Use the buttons to change the number of workers.

steps.headline: Size a pool for 260 messages a second when one worker handles 60 a second.

workedSteps.text: Arrivals must not exceed total capacity, so the pool needs at least arrivals divided by one worker's rate.
Workers are whole, so round up. Say how many are needed.

reveal.text: Round up whatever the fraction is, because a pool short by a fraction of a worker still loses ground.

steps.headline: Four workers against 270 arrivals a second, handling 60 a second each.

workedSteps.text: Total capacity is 4 × 60.
Arrivals exceed capacity, so the backlog gains the difference every second. Work out the gain over 5 minutes, which is 300 seconds.

reveal.text: A pool needs spare capacity so it can drain a backlog as well as keep up with new arrivals.

lessons.orientation: Scaling up and out, stateless tiers and load balancers, queues, and sizing a worker pool from rates.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson turns to cost and pricing, and works out what a design costs from stated prices.

blocks.text: Messages arrive at a service at 120 a second, and each worker that processes them can handle 50 a second. Two workers manage 100 a second between them and three manage 150, and how the service behaves under that load depends on comparing those figures with the arrival rate, second by second, for as long as the load lasts.

That comparison of two rates is behind most decisions about scaling in the cloud, such as how many machines to run, whether to put a queue in front of them so that work can wait instead of being lost, and whether the machines are alike enough to be swapped for one another. Once you can make it, you can say how many workers a load needs, how large a backlog grows during a burst and how long it takes to clear afterwards.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out how many workers a given load needs, predict how fast a backlog builds, and say what a load balancer and a queue each remove.
intro.whyItMatters: Most scaling failures come from a rate that was never compared with capacity.

recap.keyIdea: Capacity must exceed the arrival rate, and stateless servers behind a load balancer and queues between components let the system scale and fail in parts.

blocks.text: Scaling up has a ceiling and leaves one machine to fail, whereas scaling out adds machines and needs a stateless tier so that any of them can serve any request. A load balancer spreads requests and removes servers that fail their health checks.

A queue lets producers and consumers work at their own pace, but it hides a slow consumer only for as long as the backlog is bounded, which makes sizing the pool essential. The number of workers is the arrival rate divided by one worker's rate, rounded up.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson prices these designs, and shows where the bill comes from.

lessons.title: Cost and pricing

steps.headline: Cloud charges follow usage, so a bill splits into compute, storage, transfer and requests that can each be estimated.

lead.text: Cloud pricing follows the pay-per-use characteristic from the first lesson: you are charged for what you consume, so cost is a function of design. A bill splits into a few kinds of line. **Compute** is charged by the hour or the second, **storage** by the gigabyte for each month, **data transfer** by the gigabyte that leaves the provider network, and **requests** by the million. Each is quantity times price, and a bill is the sum of them.

The figure draws an illustrative bill from November 2026, with three virtual machines at $0.10 an hour, 500 GB stored at $0.023 per GB-month and 2,000 GB sent out at $0.09 per GB. Compute is 3 × 0.10 × 730 = $219.00, storage is $11.50 and transfer is $180.00, which makes $410.50. Switching to the second view shows that stopping the machines outside working hours takes compute down to $66.00.

afterFigure.text: Compute is not always the largest line. In this bill the transfer is nearly as large, and a design that sends large files to users will find it larger still.

diagram.alt: A monthly bill drawn as bars for compute, storage and data transfer out. Three views: the baseline at $410.50, the same bill after the virtual machines run only in working hours at $257.50, and the bill after adding a NAT gateway at $488.35.

steps.headline: Price the data leaving and add it to storage.

workedSteps.text: Data leaving the provider network is charged per gigabyte, and data coming in is usually free. Price 1,500 GB at $0.09 per GB.
Add the transfer to the storage line of $14.95. Work out the total.

reveal.text: The next screen lists this and other charges that catch teams out.

steps.headline: Transfer, NAT gateways, orphaned volumes and logs are the charges that most often surprise a team.

lead.text: Most bills that surprise a team do so through a few repeated causes. **Data transfer out** is the first: sending data to the internet, or across regions, is charged per gigabyte, whereas data coming in is usually free, so a service that serves large files pays for every download. A **NAT gateway** is the second, since it is charged an hourly fee and a fee for each gigabyte that passes through it, and a private subnet that sends a lot of traffic through one can pay more for the gateway than for the servers behind it. Illustrative prices of $0.045 an hour and $0.045 per GB make a gateway that moves 1,000 GB in a month cost 0.045 × 730 + 0.045 × 1,000 = $77.85.

The third is the **orphaned resource**: a volume whose machine was deleted, a snapshot nobody needs, or a stopped machine whose disk still exists, none of which stops billing until someone removes it. The fourth is logging, because logs are priced by the gigabyte ingested and stored, and a verbose setting can produce more of them than anyone reads. None of these is hard to avoid once seen, and all of them are visible in a bill that is broken down by line.

reveal.text: The same working shows why scheduling matters most for machines that are idle for most of the day.

steps.headline: Tags, budgets and alerts let the people who make cost decisions see them.

lead.text: Cost follows from architectural decisions, so the engineers who make them need to see the result, and the practice of managing cloud cost is called FinOps. Three basic controls support it. **Tags** are labels such as team or project attached to resources, so that a bill can be split by who caused each part. A **budget** sets an expected monthly amount, and an **alert** warns people when spending is heading past it, before the invoice arrives and not after. A regular look at the largest lines and at unused resources completes the set.
The misconception to avoid is that cost is the finance department's task. Finance can see the total, but it is the person who chooses a gateway, a storage class or an instance size who can change it.

steps.headline: Commitment pricing lowers the rate in return for steady use, and pays off above a break-even level of use.

lead.text: Providers offer capacity in three ways. **On demand** is the full price, charged for the time used and cancelled at will. **Commitment pricing**, in AWS the Savings Plans and reserved instances, gives a lower rate in return for a promise of steady usage over a term of one or three years. **Interruptible capacity**, called Spot in AWS, is spare capacity sold at a deep discount that the provider can take back at short notice, which suits work that can stop and restart.

A commitment is paid for whether it is used or not, which gives it a break-even point. With an illustrative 40% discount you pay 60% of the full price for the month whatever you do, while on demand costs the full price times the share of the month you use. The two are equal when the share used is 60%, as the figure shows: below it the commitment wastes money, above it the commitment saves.

diagram.alt: A chart of monthly cost against how much of the month a machine is used. On demand rises from zero to $73 at full use, while a commitment is a flat line, and the lines cross at 60 percent for a 40 percent discount and at 75 percent for a 25 percent discount.
