workedSteps.text: The commitment costs the full price less the discount, and it is paid for the whole month, whether the machine runs or not.
On demand costs the full price times the share of the month used, so the two cost the same when the share used equals the share paid. Work out that percentage.

reveal.text: A committed rate is a bet on steady demand, which is why it suits the baseline load and not the peaks.

lessons.orientation: Estimating a bill from usage, the charges that surprise teams, basic cost controls and commitment pricing.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson names the six Well-Architected pillars and evaluates a design for its trade-offs.

blocks.text: At an illustrative $0.023 per GB-month, 500 GB of storage costs $11.50 a month, while sending 2,000 GB to the internet at $0.09 per GB costs $180.00. The stored data is a small cost and the same data sent away is a large one, and the difference comes from data transfer, which providers charge for in one direction only.

A cloud bill is a list of quantities multiplied by prices, for hours of compute, gigabytes stored and gigabytes sent, so a design can be priced before it is built and its expensive parts found while they are still cheap to change. The prices quoted are illustrative and dated November 2026, and the same multiplication works with whatever a provider charges today.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate a monthly bill from stated usage and prices, name the charges that surprise teams, and say when a commitment is worth it.
intro.whyItMatters: A bill is a result of design, and it is far cheaper to find a cost driver on paper than on an invoice.

recap.keyIdea: A bill is quantity times price for compute, storage, transfer and requests, and the savings come from removing idle resources and committing only to steady use.

blocks.text: Pay per use means a bill is the sum of quantities times prices, so 500 GB at $0.023 is $11.50 and 2,000 GB out at $0.09 is $180.00. Data transfer out, NAT gateways, orphaned volumes and logs are the lines that most often surprise a team, and stopping a machine does not stop the charge for its disk.

Tags, budgets and alerts let engineers see the cost of their own choices. A commitment is cheaper only above a break-even level of use, 60% for a 40% discount, so it fits the steady baseline and on demand fits the rest.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson gathers cost, security, reliability and the other concerns into the six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework.

lessons.title: The Well-Architected view

steps.headline: The Well-Architected Framework organises design questions under six pillars, and the first three concern running, protecting and recovering a system.

lead.text: Providers publish guidance on how to build well, and AWS's is the Well-Architected Framework, a set of questions organised under six **pillars**. **Operational excellence** is about running systems and improving how they are run, which in practice means describing operations as code, watching what the system does and learning from every failure. **Security** is about protecting information and systems through a strong identity foundation, least privilege, encryption and detection, all of which the earlier lessons began.

**Reliability** is about a workload doing its job correctly and consistently, including recovering from failure and meeting demand, and it draws on the zone, availability and recovery ideas already met. Each pillar comes with design principles of this kind, and they are the part to remember: the pillar's name says the topic, and the principles say what to do about it.

steps.headline: The last three pillars concern using resources well, spending sensibly and reducing environmental impact.

lead.text: **Performance efficiency** is about using computing resources well for the workload and continuing to do so as demand and technology change, for example by trying a new instance type or a managed service when it fits better. **Cost optimisation** is about delivering the value the business needs at the lowest price, and it is the pillar the cost lesson belonged to: consumption pricing, removing idle resources, and understanding where the money goes.

**Sustainability**, which AWS added as the sixth pillar in 2021, is about reducing the environmental impact of running workloads, mostly by using fewer resources more fully. It overlaps with cost optimisation, since a machine that is off costs nothing and uses no power. The overlap is a reminder that the pillars are lenses on one design and not separate departments.

reveal.text: Several earlier lessons were largely about this pillar, which is why it can feel the most familiar.
The next screens put a small design through a review.

steps.headline: Strengthening one pillar usually costs another, so a design should record what it chose.

lead.text: No design maximises every pillar at once. Moving a database from one self-managed server to a managed database across two zones raises reliability and operational excellence, because the provider handles the failover and the patching, and it raises the bill. Adding a second region raises reliability further and costs more again, in money and in the complexity of keeping two regions in step. The chart gives illustrative scores from one to five for a single design as it changes, and the polygon moves outward on some axes and inward on others.

A **trade-off** is that exchange, and the discipline is to make it knowingly. A choice is good when it serves what the workload needs and its cost to the other pillars is understood and accepted, so there is no single best architecture; the right one depends on the goals. Writing the trade-off beside the choice also lets a later reader judge whether it still holds.

afterFigure.text: Some practices help two pillars together. Removing idle resources lowers cost and also removes things that can fail.

Moving the database to a multi-zone managed service raises reliability and operations and lowers cost. Adding a second region raises reliability again and lowers cost and sustainability.

steps.headline: Review a web app: two zones behind a load balancer, a managed database with a standby, and an automated release pipeline.

workedSteps.text: Start with the pipeline. Releasing by script makes operations repeatable and testable, which is the first pillar.
The managed database with a standby takes patching and failover off the team, and survives a zone loss. That serves reliability, at some cost in control over tuning.
Now the servers in two zones. Ask which pillar the choice mainly serves.

steps.headline: Continue the review: the team also encrypts all data and switches test servers off at night.

workedSteps.text: Encrypting data with managed keys protects it on disk and in transit, which is the second pillar.
Switching test servers off outside working hours removes idle charges. Name the pillar this mainly serves.

steps.headline: A review is a structured set of questions that finds risks early, and it is a method rather than a certificate.

lead.text: An **architecture review** works through the pillars as questions, such as how a system is monitored, who can reach its data, what happens when a zone fails, and where the money goes. Its purpose is to find risks before an incident does, and to leave behind a short list of decisions and the reasons for them. AWS offers a tool for recording the answers, but the value lies in the conversation and not in any score.

The Well-Architected Framework is therefore not a certification checklist, and it does not say that one architecture is right. Other providers publish comparable guidance: Microsoft's Azure Well-Architected Framework and Google Cloud's Architecture Framework organise very similar questions under their own pillars, so the habit carries over from one provider to another.

reveal.text: The workload's own goals are the standard; the framework asks you to name them and not to maximise a pillar.

lessons.orientation: The six Well-Architected pillars, trade-offs between them, and how to review a design.
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson applies encryption, audit logging and account structure, the main security controls of a cloud design.

blocks.text: An architecture review asks plain questions about a running system: how you would know it had gone wrong, who can reach its data, what happens when an availability zone fails, and where the money goes each month. AWS has collected questions of this kind into its **Well-Architected Framework**, and Microsoft and Google publish comparable frameworks of their own, so the same questions apply to a design on any of the three.

The answers rarely all improve together, since a change that makes a system harder to break usually makes it dearer or more complex to run, and a change that saves money usually gives something up. Asking the questions in a fixed order lets you see which of those exchanges a design has made, and decide whether each one suits what the workload is for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the six pillars, say which pillar a design choice serves, and state the trade-off it makes.
intro.whyItMatters: A named trade-off turns a design opinion into something a team can check against the workload's goals.

recap.keyIdea: A design is judged against six pillars, and because strengthening one usually costs another, the right design is the one whose trade-offs fit the workload's goals.

blocks.text: The six pillars are operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability, and each comes with design principles that say what to do. A choice such as a second region improves one pillar and costs another, so the design should record the trade-off it made.

A review is a structured set of questions that finds risks before they become incidents. It is a method and not a certification, there is no single best architecture, and some practices, such as removing idle resources, help two pillars at once.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes the security pillar further, with encryption, audit logs and the structure of accounts.

lessons.title: Security and governance in the cloud

steps.headline: A leaked bucket is usually one failure of three, and each failure has its own control.

lead.text: Many cloud data leaks begin the same way: a storage bucket is left readable by anyone, and someone finds it. Three separate controls address what went wrong, and they are worth keeping apart because each stops a different failure. **Access control**, meaning policies and the Block Public Access setting, decides who may read the data at all. **Encryption** protects the data itself if it is read in some way that the policy did not foresee, such as a copied disk. **Audit logging** records every call, so that when something does go wrong there is a record of what happened.

A common error is to treat one as a substitute for another. A bucket that is encrypted and open to the world is still open, because the service decrypts the data for whoever the policy admits. This is the shared responsibility line again, since the provider offers all three controls and the customer has to turn them on and set them correctly.

diagram.alt: A table of three failures with the control that stops each: block public access for an open bucket, encryption for a stolen copy, and audit logging for not knowing who changed something.
diagram.caption: Each control stops a different failure, and none of them replaces the others.

steps.headline: Data is encrypted at rest on disk and in transit on the wire, and whoever holds the key decides who can read it.

lead.text: **Encryption at rest** scrambles stored data with a key, so a copied disk or snapshot is unreadable without it. **Encryption in transit** protects data crossing a network, and for web traffic it is TLS, the protocol behind HTTPS. Amazon S3 now encrypts new objects by default, so the useful question is not whether the data is encrypted but who holds the key and who may use it.

That question is answered by **key management**. A managed key service, which in AWS is KMS, creates and stores keys, and a **key policy** says which principals may use each one. With keys the customer controls, disabling or deleting a key makes the data it protects unreadable, and every use of a key is recorded in the audit log. Encryption is therefore best seen as moving the question of access from the data to the key.

reveal.text: The next screen shows what one record in that log contains.

steps.headline: An audit log records each API call with the principal, the action, the time, the source address and the outcome.

lead.text: Every action in a cloud account, from a console click to a call by a program, is a request to the provider's API, and an **audit log** keeps an append-only record of them. In AWS it is CloudTrail. By default it keeps recent management events for 90 days, and a *trail* stores them for longer in a bucket you choose, ideally in a separate account that the people being logged cannot alter.

Each record answers the questions an investigator asks. The figure shows one event: userIdentity says *who*, eventName and eventSource say *what*, eventTime says *when*, sourceIPAddress says *from where*, and the presence of an errorCode shows that the call was refused. Failed calls are recorded as well as successful ones, which matters, because a run of refusals is often the first sign of someone probing.

afterFigure.text: The misconception is that logging can wait until there is an incident. It cannot, since a log that was not switched on cannot be read afterwards.

steps.headline: Separate accounts contain mistakes and attackers, and organisation-wide guardrails stop the worst actions.

lead.text: An account is the strongest isolation boundary a provider offers: a user, a role or a resource in one account has no access to another unless it is explicitly granted. Keeping production, development and security tooling in separate accounts means that a mistake in development cannot delete production data and a compromised developer credential reaches only what that account holds. The idea is to limit the **blast radius**, the amount that one failure can damage. A single large account is simpler to start with and is the worse choice for exactly the reason that everything is in it.

Accounts are grouped into an organisation, and the organisation can attach a **service control policy** to any account or group of accounts. A service control policy never grants access; it sets the *maximum* that anyone in those accounts can be granted, whatever their own policies say. A common use is the guardrail in the figure, which forbids switching off audit logging anywhere, and which an administrator inside an account cannot undo.

diagram.alt: An organisation containing separate production, development and security accounts, with a guardrail policy applied to all of them. One view shows a developer starting a test server, which is allowed. The other shows the developer trying to switch off audit logging, which the guardrail blocks.
diagram.caption: Accounts separate what can be damaged, and the guardrail limits what anyone may do. Use the buttons to try each action.

steps.headline: Back at the shared responsibility line, the security work of the customer is a short list of controls to turn on.

lead.text: The first lesson said that the provider secures the cloud itself and the customer secures what they put in it. This lesson fills in the customer's side as a list that a team can check. Block public access and keep policies narrow, following the least privilege rule from the IAM lesson. Encrypt data at rest and in transit, and decide who holds the keys. Switch audit logging on in every account, and send it to somewhere that cannot be altered by the people it records. Separate accounts by purpose, and set guardrails that apply to all of them.

None of these items is exotic, and most are settings that cost little. The failures that reach the news are overwhelmingly one of them left unset, which is why the customer side of the line deserves as much attention as the provider's.

reveal.text: The same mechanism can restrict the regions in which resources may be created, or require encryption.

lessons.orientation: Encryption, key management, audit logging and account structure as customer-side security controls.
lessons.reviewLabel: Security and governance in the cloud
lessons.nextAction: The next lesson picks a disaster recovery strategy for stated RTO and RPO and traces failures through a three-tier design.

blocks.text: A storage bucket holding customer records is encrypted, backed up and replicated across regions, and it is also readable by anyone who knows its address. The encryption does nothing to prevent that, since the storage service decrypts the data for every reader its policy admits, so the records are exposed however carefully they were protected against loss.

A cloud design guards its data with several kinds of control, among them access control, encryption, logging and the separation of workloads into accounts, and each kind stops one particular failure while leaving the others untouched. Knowing which failure each one addresses lets you look at a design and see which control it is missing, as the bucket above is missing a limit on who may read it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose the control that stops a given exposure, read an audit log event, and say how accounts and guardrails limit damage.
intro.whyItMatters: Most cloud breaches come from a control left unset, and each control here is a setting the customer owns.

recap.keyIdea: Access control, encryption and audit logging each stop a different failure, and separate accounts with guardrails limit how far any one failure reaches.

blocks.text: Encryption protects data at rest and in transit, and the holder of the key decides who can read it, but it does not replace an access policy. Audit logs record who did what, when and from where, including the calls that failed, and they must be switched on before an incident.

Separate accounts limit the blast radius of a mistake or a compromise, and a service control policy bounds what anyone in them may be granted. The customer's half of shared responsibility is largely this list of controls, turned on and set correctly.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these controls inside a design built to survive failure, and sets out the four recovery strategies.

lessons.title: Designing for failure and disaster recovery

steps.headline: There are four recovery strategies, and each buys a shorter recovery with more running infrastructure.

lead.text: A disaster recovery plan says what happens if a whole region is lost, and AWS describes four strategies in order. **Backup and restore** keeps only copies of data in another region, so everything else, the servers and the network, is rebuilt after the disaster, which is the cheapest and slowest. **Pilot light** also keeps the core data services running and up to date in the second region, with the servers switched off until they are needed. **Warm standby** runs a complete but scaled-down copy of the system, which is scaled up when it has to take over. **Multi-site active/active** runs a full copy in both regions, both serving users.

Moving down the list, more of the system is already running when the disaster arrives, so the recovery time shrinks from hours to minutes to almost nothing, and the cost rises with it. The figure draws the primary and recovery regions for each, with bars for the relative recovery time and cost.

diagram.alt: Four disaster recovery strategies, drawn as a primary region and a recovery region. Backup and restore keeps only copies of data. Pilot light adds core data services running. Warm standby runs a scaled-down full copy. Multi-site active/active runs a full copy that serves traffic.
diagram.caption: From the first to the fourth, recovery gets faster and the bill grows. Use the buttons to compare the strategies.

reveal.text: The question that decides between the four is how much of the system must already be running when the disaster arrives.

steps.headline: The strategy is chosen from the stated RTO and RPO, and active/active is justified only by strict targets.

lead.text: The choice starts from the recovery time objective and recovery point objective of the previous database lesson. Backup and restore suits targets of hours, pilot light suits tens of minutes, warm standby suits minutes, and active/active suits targets near zero. The strategy should be the cheapest one that meets the targets, so a system with a 4-hour RTO and a 1-hour RPO on a modest budget suits pilot light or warm standby and does not need active/active.

The misconception to avoid is that multi-region active/active is the default. It costs the most, and it adds the work of keeping two regions consistent, so it is justified only where the business will pay for near-zero recovery. A second misconception is that having backups means being able to recover: restoring from nothing takes the longest, and a restore that has never been tried may not work.

steps.headline: Pick a strategy for an RTO of 10 minutes and an RPO of 1 minute, where one region serving traffic at a time is acceptable.

workedSteps.text: An RTO of 10 minutes rules out backup and restore, which takes hours, and pilot light, which usually takes tens of minutes.
Active/active would meet it, but it pays for a second fully loaded region to reach a target that is not near zero.
The cheapest strategy left runs a scaled-down full copy that is scaled up at disaster time. Name it.

steps.headline: Pick a strategy for an RTO of 24 hours and an RPO of 12 hours, on a very small budget.

workedSteps.text: Both targets are measured in hours, so there is time to rebuild the system after a disaster.
Name the cheapest strategy, which keeps only copies of data in another region.

steps.headline: A three-tier design puts every tier in two zones, so that any single failure leaves the service running.

lead.text: A typical design has three tiers. A load balancer receives requests and passes them to a **web tier** of stateless servers, which call an **application tier**, which reads and writes a **data tier**, a database with a primary and a standby. Each tier is placed in at least two availability zones, so the loss of one zone removes half of every tier at most, and the load balancer stops sending requests to the failed half.

Trace the failures in the figure. When zone b fails, the web and application servers in zone a carry on, and the database standby is promoted if the primary was the thing lost. When only the database primary fails, the standby in the other zone takes over and the upper tiers do not notice. The design rides through a zone failure without an outage, which is the thing a well-built system should do, and it needs enough capacity in the surviving zone to carry the load.

diagram.alt: A three-tier system spread over two zones: a load balancer, a stateless web tier, an application tier and a database with a primary in zone a and a standby in zone b. Views show normal running, the loss of zone b, and the failure of the database primary.
diagram.caption: Each tier is present in both zones, so any single failure leaves the service up. Use the buttons to fail a part.

steps.headline: Surviving the loss of one zone requires spare capacity, and spreading over more zones makes it cheaper.

lead.text: The surviving zones must carry the whole peak, which fixes the number of servers. With two zones, each must carry the full peak alone, so a peak that takes 4 servers needs 4 in each zone, 8 in all, and the spare capacity is 100%. With three zones, any two must carry the peak, so each zone carries half of it: for a peak that needs 6 servers, each zone runs 3, and 9 run in total, which is spare capacity of 50%.

The rule is that the servers per zone are the peak divided by the number of zones that remain after a loss, which is one fewer than the zones in use, and the total is that figure times the number of zones. More zones therefore reduce the extra cost of surviving one failure, until the added complexity of managing them outweighs the saving.

reveal.text: Compare the answer with the figure of 16 that two zones would need for the same peak.

steps.headline: Recovery that has not been rehearsed is only a hope, so failures are practised on purpose.

lead.text: A plan that has never been run tends to fail where nobody looked: a restore that takes longer than the RTO, a permission that was never granted in the recovery region, a runbook that names a person who has left. The remedy is to rehearse. A **game day** is a planned exercise in which the team causes a failure, such as stopping a zone's servers or failing over the database, and watches whether the system and the people respond as designed. The results are written down and fixed, and the exercise is repeated.

The same applies to backups, which should be restored from time to time and timed against the RTO. Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* book makes the general point that reliability comes from engineering for failure and testing it, and the cloud makes this practical, since a test environment can be built, broken and removed for a few dollars.

reveal.text: More zones cut the spare capacity, and rehearsing the loss of a zone is what shows that the surviving ones really do carry the load.

lessons.orientation: The four recovery strategies, choosing one from RTO and RPO, a three-tier design across zones, and rehearsing failure.
lessons.reviewLabel: Designing for failure and disaster recovery
lessons.nextAction: You can now describe a cloud system's responsibilities, availability, access, network, compute, storage, cost and recovery, and review a design against the pillars.

blocks.text: A business that can do without its service for four hours after losing a whole region, and can afford to lose one hour of data, has stated an [[RTO|Recovery time objective: the longest outage the business will accept. Met in 'Databases and recovery objectives'.]] of four hours and an [[RPO|Recovery point objective: how much recent data the business will accept losing, measured in time. Met in 'Databases and recovery objectives'.]] of one. Those two figures decide how much of the system must already be standing in a second region before anything goes wrong, anywhere from copies of the data alone to a full second copy serving users.

Meeting them costs money in two places. Across regions, the shorter the recovery time, the more of the system has to be running in advance, and inside a region, surviving the loss of a zone means running servers that are partly idle on an ordinary day. A **disaster recovery** design sets both costs against the targets, so that you pay for the readiness the business needs and no more.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to pick a recovery strategy for stated RTO and RPO, work out the capacity that surviving a zone loss requires, and trace a failure through a three-tier design.
intro.whyItMatters: This is where the availability, database and cost ideas of the course meet in one design decision.

recap.keyIdea: Choose the cheapest recovery strategy that meets the stated RTO and RPO, and build each tier across zones with enough spare capacity to ride through a failure.

blocks.text: The four strategies are backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active/active, in falling recovery time and rising cost, and the right one is the cheapest that meets the stated RTO and RPO. A three-tier design with every tier in two or more zones rides through the loss of a zone, provided the surviving zones can carry the peak.

That capacity is the peak divided by the zones that remain, times the zones in use, so more zones cost less to protect. Whatever the design, it is only a hope until the restore and the failover have been rehearsed.

questions.prompt: A bill lists 41 hours of virtual machine time used last month, and nothing for the hours the machine was off. Which of the five characteristics produces a bill like that?
hints: Think about which characteristic is about counting use.
The bill follows what was consumed rather than what was installed.
questions.onCorrect: Metering also lets a provider report usage to customers and to its own capacity planning.

misconceptions.feedback: Elasticity is about capacity growing and shrinking. The characteristic that produces a bill from recorded use is a different one.

questions.prompt: A company moves its customer database from its own server room onto virtual machines in the cloud. Who is now responsible for deciding who may read the data in that database?
hints: Ask who chooses the settings, not who owns the building.
The provider secures the platform; what you put on it is yours.
questions.onCorrect: Access to your data is a setting you choose, so it stays with you however the hardware is run.

choices.label: The provider, since it owns the hardware
The provider and the company, split equally
Nobody, since the database is encrypted by default

misconceptions.feedback: Owning the hardware makes the provider responsible for the hardware. Decisions about who may read your data are made by the customer.
The split is not an equal share. It follows the layers: the provider runs the lower ones and the customer runs what is placed on them.
Encryption helps, but someone still decides who holds the keys and who may sign in. Those decisions belong to the customer.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, who patches the guest operating system of an EC2 instance?
hints: The operating system sits inside the virtual machine you rent.
Look at which side of the line it falls on under IaaS.
questions.onCorrect: The guest OS runs inside the machine you rent, so patching it is part of using IaaS.

misconceptions.feedback: The hypervisor underneath is run for you, but the operating system inside the instance is the part you rent and keep up to date under IaaS.

questions.prompt: Under RDS, who patches the operating system of the database server, the provider or the customer?
hints: Compare with EC2: what did the customer give up by choosing a managed database?
Think about which side of the line a managed service takes on.
questions.onCorrect: RDS moves the operating system and engine patching to the provider; the customer still sets who may connect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the EC2 answer. With a managed database the other side takes over the server layers.

questions.prompt: Under RDS, who decides which networks and people may connect to the database, the provider or the customer?
hints: Moving a layer to the provider does not move your data.
Access settings control your data.
questions.onCorrect: However much of the stack the provider runs, access to your data stays a customer setting.

misconceptions.feedback: The controls are offered for you, but you decide how they are set. A managed service does not choose that for you.

questions.prompt: You upload your application code to a service that creates the servers, installs the runtime and patches the operating system for you. You never log in to a machine. What is this service model called?
hints: Which layers did the provider take over?
You still supply the application and its data.
questions.onCorrect: AWS Elastic Beanstalk is one example: you supply code, and it provisions and patches what runs it.

misconceptions.feedback: With the infrastructure model you would still manage the operating system. Here someone else manages it too.
With SaaS you would use finished software instead of uploading your own application.

questions.prompt: A company uses a hosted email product (SaaS) and nothing else. Of the seven layers in the stack, from the facility up to the data, which does the company still manage?
hints: SaaS runs the application for you.
Ask what the company puts into the service that nobody else could supply.

acceptedIdeas: Only the data, with the settings for who may use it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the data, with the settings for who may use it

questions.onCorrect: The data is the one layer that stays with the customer, together with the sign-in and sharing settings around it.

choices.label: Only the data, with the settings for who may use it
The operating system and everything above it
None, since the provider runs all seven

misconceptions.feedback: The operating system and everything above it is where the line falls for IaaS. Under SaaS the operating system, the runtime and the application are all run for you.
The application is the product being rented, so under SaaS it is run for you along with everything beneath it.
The software is run for you, but the messages themselves and the choice of who may read them stay with the company.

questions.prompt: You rent a virtual machine and install your own database on it. Which service model is this?
hints: Who installs and maintains the operating system?
Renting raw machines is the most basic model.
questions.onCorrect: You manage the operating system and everything above it, which is the split this model makes.

misconceptions.feedback: A platform model would give you a ready runtime to deploy code to. Here you install the database yourself on a machine.
A software model delivers finished software. Here you are building the setup yourself.
Functions as a service runs your code without servers to manage. A machine you set up yourself is the more basic model.

questions.prompt: In EC2, who patches the guest operating system, the provider or the customer?
hints: EC2 is IaaS.
Under IaaS the operating system is the first layer above the hypervisor that you control.
questions.onCorrect: Under IaaS the guest operating system is the customer's job.

misconceptions.feedback: Whoever you rent from patches what runs beneath the instance, not the operating system inside it.

questions.prompt: How many essential characteristics does the NIST definition of cloud computing list?
hints: Count: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, and two more.
The last two are about capacity growing and shrinking, and about metering.
Add them up: three named plus the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The five are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

questions.onCorrect: NIST lists five essential characteristics, three service models and four deployment models.

misconceptions.feedback: Three is the number of service models. The characteristics are more numerous.
Four is the number of deployment models. The characteristics number one more.

questions.prompt: Six web servers are spread evenly over three availability zones, two in each. One zone loses power. What happens to the web servers?
hints: A zone has its own power, cooling and network.
Ask how many servers sit in the zone that failed.

acceptedIdeas: The two in that zone stop, and the other four keep running
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two in that zone stop, and the other four keep running

questions.onCorrect: Losing one zone costs a third of the capacity here, so the remaining servers have to be enough for the load.

choices.label: The two in that zone stop, and the other four keep running
None stop, since the zone switches to another zone's power
All six stop, since the zones are in one region
Three stop, since half the region's power is lost

misconceptions.feedback: The zones share a region but not a building or a power supply, so a failure in one leaves the others running.
A zone's failure reaches only the servers inside it, and each zone here holds a third of the servers.
Each zone has its own power, so the servers inside the failed zone go down with it, and the design survives because the other zones carry on.

questions.prompt: Two components are both needed for a request to succeed, and each one is available 99.9% of the time. Compared with 99.9%, the availability of the pair is
hints: Does the request need one component or both?
Each component can fail on its own, and either failure stops the request.

acceptedIdeas: lower, because either one failing breaks the request
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: lower, because either one failing breaks the request

questions.onCorrect: Each required component adds its own chance of failure, so the total goes down.

choices.label: higher, because there are two of them
impossible to tell without the failure times
lower, because either one failing breaks the request

misconceptions.feedback: Two copies help only when either can serve alone. Here both are required.
Identical components do not cancel. Each one adds its own chance of failure.
The availability of the pair can be worked out from the two figures: when both must work, the two multiply.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: what is the availability of the web tier and database in series, as a percentage?
hints: Write each availability as a decimal first.
Multiply 0.9995 by 0.999.
Multiply the decimal by 100 to give a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The result is lower than either component, as it must be when both are required.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weaker component alone. Both are required, so multiply the two availabilities.
That is one component alone. The pair is lower than either.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: what is the availability of the redundant pair, as a percentage?
hints: The pair fails only when both copies fail at once.
Each copy fails 0.5% of the time, which is 0.005 as a decimal.
Square 0.005 and subtract it from 1, then convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Redundancy turns two modest components into one that fails once in 40,000 periods, if failures are independent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a single copy. The second copy is what raises it.
That subtracts the two failure rates, which overstates the failure chance. Multiply them instead.

questions.prompt: A load balancer with 99.99% availability sits in series with a redundant pair of web servers, each 99.9% available and failing independently. The load balancer must work, and either server will do. What is the availability of the whole, as a percentage?
hints: Work out the pair first: both servers must fail for the pair to fail.
The pair is 1 − 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.999999. Then combine it with the balancer.
Multiply 0.9999 by 0.999999 and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The balancer is now the weakest link, so improving the web servers further would barely change the total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the pair alone. The balancer is also required, so it multiplies in.
That is the balancer alone. The pair lowers the total a little.

questions.prompt: Two required components each have 99.9% availability and fail independently. What is the availability of the pair in series, as a percentage?
hints: Both components must work, so the availabilities multiply.
Write 99.9% as 0.999 and multiply 0.999 by 0.999.
Convert the product back to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Every extra required component multiplies in another factor below one, so the whole is lower than any part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one component. The pair needs both, so multiply.
Subtracting 0.1 twice drops a small term. Multiply 0.999 × 0.999 to get the exact figure.

questions.prompt: A service must have 99.99% availability over a year of 525,600 minutes. How many minutes of downtime are allowed?
hints: 99.99% leaves 0.01% unavailable.
As a decimal 0.01% is 0.0001.
Multiply 525,600 by 0.0001.
questions.onCorrect: Four nines allows under an hour of downtime in a year; five nines allows about five minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the unavailable share as 1%. Here it is 0.01%.
That is the figure for 99.999%. Four nines leaves 0.01%.

questions.prompt: Where should two web servers be placed so that the service survives the loss of one data centre?
hints: A zone is the unit that fails together.
Which option keeps a server alive after any one zone is lost?

acceptedIdeas: In two availability zones of one region
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In two availability zones of one region

questions.onCorrect: Zones within a region are isolated from each other and linked by low-latency networking, which is why they are the usual redundancy unit.

choices.label: On one larger server in one zone
In two availability zones of one region
In one zone, with backups of the data

misconceptions.feedback: Both servers share one zone, so one zone failure removes both.
A single machine is a single point of failure, however large it is.
Backups help recovery of data, but the service is down until something runs again.

questions.prompt: No policy mentions ec2:StopInstances, and a user asks to stop an instance. What happens to the request?
hints: Think about what a policy has to say before something is permitted.
Silence in policies is not permission.

acceptedIdeas: It is denied, since nothing allows it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is denied, since nothing allows it

questions.onCorrect: Default deny is why a new user with no policies can do nothing at all.

choices.label: It is denied, since nothing allows it
It is allowed, since nothing forbids it
It is allowed only if the user is an administrator

misconceptions.feedback: IAM does not treat silence as permission, so a request that no policy permits is refused.
Being an administrator is itself a matter of policies, and with no policy that mentions this action there is nothing to permit the request.

questions.prompt: Two policies apply. One allows s3:GetObject on reports/*. The other denies s3:GetObject on reports/secret/*. Four requests arrive: (1) GetObject on reports/q1.csv, (2) GetObject on reports/secret/q3.csv, (3) PutObject on reports/q2.csv, (4) GetObject on reports/secret/keys.txt. Which of them are allowed?
hints: Check each request for an explicit deny first, then for an allow.
PutObject is a different action from GetObject.
questions.onCorrect: Request 1 is the only one with a matching allow and no deny.

misconceptions.feedback: Request (3) is a PutObject, and the only allow names GetObject, so nothing permits it and it is refused by default.
Requests (2) and (4) fall under reports/secret/, where the explicit deny matches, and a deny overrides the allow.
The deny covers (2) and (4), and no statement permits PutObject, so (3) is refused by default as well.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: is the PutObject request allowed or denied?
hints: Does any statement name s3:PutObject?
If no statement matches, no allow was found.
questions.onCorrect: The statement allows reading only, so writing falls through to the default.

misconceptions.feedback: The only allow names reading an object. Writing is a different action.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: is the DeleteObject request allowed or denied?
hints: Which check comes first in the order of evaluation?
One statement allows the action, and another denies it.
questions.onCorrect: An explicit deny ends the evaluation at once, whatever else allows the request.

misconceptions.feedback: The allow matches, but the evaluation checks for explicit denies first, and one matches here.

questions.prompt: A policy lets a build server call s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on 4 named buckets. A second policy lets it call every one of 12 listed S3 actions on all 4 buckets. How many more action-and-bucket combinations does the second policy grant than the first?
hints: Count the combinations in the first policy: actions times buckets.
Do the same for the second policy.
Subtract the first count from the second.
questions.onCorrect: Each unneeded action is a permission an attacker or a mistake could use, so narrower grants shrink what can go wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the second policy alone. The question asks how many more it grants.
That is the first policy. Subtract it from the second policy's total.

questions.prompt: A nightly job needs to read objects under reports/ in one bucket. Which policy follows least privilege?
hints: Compare the action list and the resource list in each option.
Which grants exactly what the job needs and nothing else?
questions.onCorrect: The job can read what it needs and nothing else, which limits the damage if its credentials leak.

choices.label: Allow s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on reports/*
Allow s3:GetObject on every object in the account

misconceptions.feedback: That grants every S3 action on every bucket, far more than reading one prefix.
The action fits, but the resource covers every object in the account.
Writing is not needed, so it is an unneeded permission.

questions.prompt: One policy allows s3:GetObject on a bucket and another explicitly denies it. The request is
hints: Evaluation looks for an explicit deny before it looks for an allow.
Does an administrator role override an explicit deny?
questions.onCorrect: An explicit deny overrides every allow, whichever policy it comes from.

choices.label: Allowed if the user is an administrator

misconceptions.feedback: The allow is found, but an explicit deny in another policy overrides it.
Being an administrator does not change the order: an explicit deny still wins unless that policy is removed.
Logging records what happened but does not decide it.

questions.prompt: What is the name of an identity that is assumed temporarily and gives short-lived credentials?
hints: It is not a person's sign-in.
A server can assume it, receiving credentials that expire.
questions.onCorrect: Roles remove the long-lived key that could otherwise be stolen from a server.

misconceptions.feedback: A user has long-lived credentials. The identity asked about is assumed and expires.

questions.prompt: What is the decision for a request when no policy mentions the action?
hints: Access has to be granted for it to exist.
Think of what a new account can do before any policy is added.
questions.onCorrect: The default is deny, which is why the rest of the rules are about what to allow.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing grants it, and access must be granted. The answer is the opposite.

questions.prompt: How many addresses does a /20 block contain?
hints: A /20 fixes 20 of the 32 bits.
The other 12 bits are free.
Work out 2 raised to the power 12.
questions.onCorrect: Each bit freed doubles the count, so a /20 holds 16 times as many addresses as a /24.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2^20, the number of fixed bits. The free bits, 32 − 20, set the count.
That is the prefix length. The count is a power of two.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: is 10.0.2.5 inside the block 10.0.1.0/24? Answer yes or no.
hints: A /24 fixes the first three numbers of the address.
Compare the third number of each.
questions.onCorrect: Only addresses starting 10.0.1 belong to 10.0.1.0/24; 10.0.2.5 belongs to 10.0.2.0/24.

misconceptions.feedback: A /24 fixes the first 24 bits, which are the three numbers 10.0.1. The third number differs.

questions.prompt: On AWS, 5 addresses in each subnet are reserved. How many are usable in a /28 subnet?
hints: A /28 leaves 4 free bits.
2^4 = 16 addresses in all.
Take away the 5 reserved.
questions.onCorrect: The reserved five are the network address, the VPC router, the DNS server, one held for future use, and the broadcast address.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every address in the block. Five are reserved by AWS.
Two reserved is the usual figure elsewhere. AWS reserves five in each subnet.

questions.prompt: A server sits in a subnet and has a public IP address, but its subnet's route table has no route to an internet gateway. Can the internet reach it?
hints: What decides where the subnet sends traffic that leaves it?
Think about whether a public address alone gives a path.

acceptedIdeas: No, because nothing routes traffic between the subnet and the internet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because nothing routes traffic between the subnet and the internet

questions.onCorrect: A public address is only half of it. Without a route to the gateway, there is no path.

choices.label: Yes, because the public address is enough
Yes, but only for web traffic on port 443
No, because nothing routes traffic between the subnet and the internet

misconceptions.feedback: A public address names the server, but traffic still needs a route between the subnet and the internet, and this table has none.
A route applies to all traffic alike, so with no route to an internet gateway no port is reachable from outside.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: which destination does the default route in a public subnet use, written as a CIDR block?
hints: It must match every address that is not inside the VPC.
A prefix length of 0 fixes no bits.
questions.onCorrect: A /0 prefix fixes nothing, so it matches any address, and a route to it catches all traffic with no more specific route.

questions.prompt: A /16 is to be divided into equal subnets of /22. How many subnets can it hold?
hints: Compare how many bits each block fixes.
The smaller blocks fix some extra bits.
Each extra bit doubles the count, so raise 2 to the number of extra bits.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing evenly this way is why prefix lengths stay in step: each extra bit halves a block.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of extra bits. Each extra bit doubles the count.
That is how many /24 subnets fit in a /16, and a /22 block is four times as large as a /24.

questions.prompt: How many addresses are in a /24 block?
hints: A /24 fixes 24 of the 32 bits.
8 bits remain free.
Work out 2 raised to the power 8.
questions.onCorrect: 256 is the size of the last number in a dotted address, which is why a /24 is the familiar neat block.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of free bits. The count is 2 raised to that power.
That is the prefix length, not the count.

questions.prompt: On AWS, 5 addresses in each subnet are reserved. How many are usable in a /26 subnet?
hints: A /26 leaves 6 free bits.
That gives 2^6 = 64 addresses.
Take away the 5 reserved.
questions.onCorrect: Small subnets lose a large share to the reserved five, which is why very small blocks are rarely worth it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the reserved addresses too. AWS keeps five.
Subtract five from the number of addresses, not from the number of free bits.

questions.prompt: What makes a subnet public?
hints: A name is only a label.
The route table decides where traffic leaves the subnet.

acceptedIdeas: Its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway

questions.onCorrect: The route and a public address on the resource are what matter; no label or size makes a subnet public.

choices.label: A network ACL that allows all traffic
Its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway

misconceptions.feedback: A name is a label for people. Nothing in the network reads it.
Size sets how many addresses there are, not where traffic can go.
A filter can allow traffic, but a route is what gives traffic a path out.

questions.prompt: A batch job needs to run continuously for six hours. Of virtual machines, containers and functions, which cannot run it in one go because of a time limit per run?
hints: One of the three options runs code only for short bursts.
AWS caps a single run of it at 15 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: A function is built for short event-driven runs; long jobs belong on a machine or in a container.

misconceptions.feedback: A virtual machine runs for as long as you keep it on. The limit belongs to the pay-per-run option.
A container runs until its process ends, with no fixed cap on duration.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: three instances at $0.10 an hour, over 730 hours. What is the monthly cost in dollars?
hints: First find the cost of one instance for the month.
One instance costs $0.10 × 730 hours.
Multiply that by the number of instances.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026. Real prices differ by instance type and region.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a single instance. The working has three.
That is the hourly total for three instances. Multiply by the hours in the month.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: a 40% commitment discount is applied to $219.00. What is the new monthly price in dollars?
hints: A 40% discount leaves 60% of the price.
Write 60% as 0.6.
Multiply 219 by 0.6.
questions.onCorrect: A commitment discount trades flexibility for price: you promise a level of use for a term and pay less per hour.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount saved. The question asks what remains to pay.
That takes off 40 dollars instead of 40 percent.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: 500,000 GB-seconds at $0.0000167 each. What is the duration charge in dollars?
hints: Multiply the GB-seconds by the price of each.
Move the decimal point carefully: 0.0000167 is 16.7 millionths.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026. Duration is usually the larger share of a function bill, and request charges are the smaller.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the request charge from the previous step. The duration charge is separate.
That is the total of both charges. The question asks for the duration charge alone.

questions.prompt: A function given 1 GB of memory costs $0.20 per million requests plus $3.34 per million for its running time, so $3.54 per million. A virtual machine costs $73.00 a month however much it serves. At how many million requests a month do the two cost the same? Give the answer to one decimal place.
hints: Add the two per-million charges for the function.
The two costs are equal when the requests, in millions, times $3.54 equal $73.00.
Divide 73 by 3.54.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.20 + 3.34 = 3.54 per million. 73.00 ÷ 3.54 ≈ 20.62, so about 20.6 million requests a month.

questions.onCorrect: Illustrative prices, November 2026. Doubling the memory doubled the running-time charge, so the crossing falls from about 39 million requests to about 21 million.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the function's price per million. Divide the machine's cost by it.
That uses the $0.20 request charge only. The running time is charged as well.
That uses the running-time charge only. Add the $0.20 per million for requests.

questions.prompt: Two instances cost $0.20 an hour each. Over 730 hours, what is the monthly cost in dollars? (Illustrative price.)
hints: Cost of one instance: its hourly price times the hours.
Multiply that by the number of instances.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one instance. There are two.
That is the hourly total. Multiply by the hours in the month.

questions.prompt: A 30% commitment discount applies to $292.00. What is the new price in dollars?
hints: A 30% discount leaves 70% of the price.
Write 70% as 0.7.
Multiply 292 by 0.7.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the amount saved. The question asks for what remains.
That subtracts 30 dollars instead of 30 percent.

questions.prompt: A job runs for 3 seconds a few times an hour and needs no servers kept warm. Which fits best?
hints: Compare how each option is billed when nothing is running.
One option charges only for the runs themselves.
questions.onCorrect: A function is billed per request and per run time, so idle hours cost nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: It would bill for every idle hour between runs.
A dedicated host is a whole physical server, reserved and billed whether used or not.
A cluster keeps capacity waiting, which a short occasional job does not need.

questions.prompt: What does serverless computing mean?
hints: Think about where the code must run in the end.
Who looks after the machines in this model?

acceptedIdeas: Servers run the code, and the provider manages them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Servers run the code, and the provider manages them

questions.onCorrect: The machines exist; the customer simply never provisions, patches or sizes them.

choices.label: Servers run the code, and the provider manages them
The code runs on the customer's own laptop
The code is stored but never executed
No physical servers are used anywhere

misconceptions.feedback: Code has to run on something. The servers exist and belong to the provider.
Serverless code runs in the provider's data centres, not on a laptop.
The provider runs the code whenever an event arrives.

questions.prompt: Many web servers must read and write the same shared directory of files at once. Which kind of storage fits: object, block or file?
hints: Think about which kind presents a folder many machines can mount.
One of the three attaches to a single machine; another is read by key over HTTP.
questions.onCorrect: File storage is mounted over the network by many machines, which is what a shared directory needs.

misconceptions.feedback: A block volume attaches to one machine at a time, so servers could not share it.
Object storage is read and replaced whole by key, not edited in place like a shared directory.

questions.prompt: A storage service has a power failure and your objects cannot be read for an hour. Afterwards every object is there again. Which statement is right?
hints: Ask separately: was the data lost, and could it be read at the time?
An object that comes back was never lost.

acceptedIdeas: Availability dropped, but durability did not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Availability dropped, but durability did not

questions.onCorrect: The two measures differ: data can be safe and still briefly out of reach.

choices.label: Durability failed, because the data was unreachable
Durability and availability are the same measure
Availability dropped, but durability did not
Neither measure is affected by an outage

misconceptions.feedback: Durability asks whether data survives, and here it did.
The outage stopped reads, which is exactly what availability measures.
They are separate: one asks if data exists, the other if it can be read now.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: with a 10^-11 chance of losing each object in a year, how many objects do you expect to lose in a year out of 10,000,000? Give a decimal.
hints: Expected losses are the number of objects times the chance for each.
Add the exponents when you multiply powers of ten.
questions.onCorrect: That is about one object every 10,000 years, which is what eleven nines of durability means in practice.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one object. Multiply by the number of objects.
That uses 10^-9; the chance is 10^-11.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: how many objects do you expect to lose in a year out of 1,000,000,000, at the same 10^-11 chance each? Give a decimal.
hints: Multiply 10^9 by 10^-11.
Write the resulting power of ten as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: A thousand times as many objects, a hundred times the expected loss, but still about one object in a century.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for 10,000,000 objects. Here there are a hundred times as many.
That treats the chance as 10^-9. It is 10^-11.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: what is the total monthly cost in dollars of 10,000 GB in the infrequent-access class, including 2,000 GB read back? (Illustrative: $0.0125 per GB-month, $0.01 per GB read.)
hints: Storage cost: 10,000 GB at $0.0125.
Retrieval cost: 2,000 GB at $0.01.
Add the two.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative prices, November 2026. The cheaper class wins only while retrieval stays low.

misconceptions.feedback: That is storage alone. The 2,000 GB read back adds a fee.
That is the standard class for the same data. This class costs less.

questions.prompt: A bucket is replicated to a second region. An engineer then deletes a folder by mistake, and the deletion is copied across as well. Which feature would have kept the deleted objects recoverable?
hints: Replication copies what the source does, including mistakes.
Which feature keeps earlier versions of an object?
questions.onCorrect: Versioning keeps earlier versions when an object is overwritten or deleted, which replication alone does not.

misconceptions.feedback: Replication is the thing that spread the deletion. A separate protection keeps earlier states.

questions.prompt: Which storage suits a database engine's data volume on one virtual machine?
hints: A database engine reads and writes small pieces of a disk constantly.
Which kind is attached to a machine as a disk?
questions.onCorrect: Block storage behaves like a local disk and can change any block in place, which database engines depend on.

misconceptions.feedback: Object storage replaces whole objects over HTTP, and cannot serve as an engine's disk.
An archive class is for rarely read data and takes hours to retrieve.
Tape is an offline archive medium, not a disk attached to a running machine.

questions.prompt: Annual loss chance per object is 10^-11. For 2,500,000,000 objects, what is the expected number of objects lost in a year? Give a decimal.
hints: Expected losses are the number of objects times the chance for each.
Multiply 2.5 by 10^9 × 10^-11, then write the result as a decimal.
questions.onCorrect: Even at that scale the expected loss is a small fraction of one object in a year.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the 10^-11 chance. Multiply by it.
The powers of ten combine to 10^-2, so the result is 2.5 hundredths.

questions.prompt: What type of storage addresses whole items by key over HTTP?
hints: It is the kind used by S3.
Its prefixes only look like folders.
questions.onCorrect: Object storage has a flat namespace of keys, which is why prefixes only look like folders.

misconceptions.feedback: Block storage is a disk attached to a machine, not addressed by key over HTTP.
File storage is mounted as a folder, not fetched by key.

questions.prompt: A shopping cart is fetched by customer ID, millions of times a second, with no joins and no ad hoc queries. Which database model fits: relational, key-value or document?
hints: Look at the access pattern: one key in, one item out.
Joins are the main thing the answer lacks.
questions.onCorrect: A key-value store keeps its speed at very large scale because every request names the item it wants.

misconceptions.feedback: Relational models earn their keep when queries join related tables, which this workload never does.
Documents suit records whose fields vary. This workload is a plain lookup by key.

questions.prompt: Backups of a database run every 8 hours, and nothing else copies its data. If the database fails, roughly how much of its most recent data could be lost in the worst case?
hints: Changes made since the last backup exist nowhere else.
Ask how old the last backup could be, at worst.

acceptedIdeas: Up to about 8 hours of changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Up to about 8 hours of changes

questions.onCorrect: The worst case is a failure just before the next backup is due, so it equals the interval.

choices.label: Up to about 16 hours of changes
Up to about 8 hours of changes

misconceptions.feedback: A backup holds the data as it was when the backup was taken, so changes made after it are in no copy at all.
Nothing copies the data between backups, so the loss can reach back to the last one, which may be hours old.
Only changes since the most recent backup are lost, and that backup is never more than one interval old.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: backups run at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00, and a failure hits at 14:20. How many minutes of changes since the last backup are lost?
hints: Find the most recent backup before 14:20.
The last backup was at 12:00.
Count the minutes from 12:00 to 14:20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The last backup was at 12:00. From 12:00 to 14:20 is 2 hours 20 minutes, which is 140 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: Only a restore to that backup is possible, so everything after 12:00 is missing.

misconceptions.feedback: Count from the last backup at 12:00, not from the one before it.
That counts from 10:00. The last backup was at 12:00.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: failure at 14:10, service restored at 15:05, and an RTO of 45 minutes. By how many minutes was the RTO missed?
hints: First work out how long the outage lasted.
Count the minutes from failure to restored service.
Subtract the allowed 45 minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The outage lasted 55 minutes against 45 allowed, so the RTO was missed by 10 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: An RTO is a ceiling on the outage, so the gap above it is the miss.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the outage length. The question asks by how much it exceeded 45.
That is the objective itself. Subtract it from the outage length.

questions.prompt: A site is slow because its database serves too many read queries. Which feature adds capacity for them: a multi-AZ standby or a read replica?
hints: One of the two cannot be read at all while the primary is healthy.
Which one exists to serve extra reads?
questions.onCorrect: A read replica serves reads from another copy, though with some replication lag.

misconceptions.feedback: A standby waits for a failover and does not serve queries while the primary is healthy.

questions.prompt: A restore plan needs 10 minutes to detect the failure, 25 minutes to restore the backup and 15 minutes to switch the application over. The RTO is 30 minutes. By how many minutes does the plan miss the RTO?
hints: The recovery time is the whole outage, not the restore alone.
Add the three stages.
Subtract the RTO from the total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 + 25 + 15 = 50 minutes of outage, and 50 − 30 = 20 minutes over.

questions.onCorrect: Detection and switch-over count toward the outage, so tuning the restore alone would not be enough.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the restore alone. Detection and switch-over are part of the outage.
That is the outage length. The question asks by how much it exceeded the RTO.

questions.prompt: Backups run every 6 hours. What is the worst-case RPO in hours?
hints: The worst case is a failure just before the next backup.
Everything since the last backup would be lost.
That is as long as the gap between backups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A failure just before the next backup loses the whole interval, 6 hours.

questions.onCorrect: Shipping transaction logs between backups is how recovery gets below the backup interval.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the interval is the average, not the worst case.
A backup protects only what existed when it ran.

questions.prompt: A failure happens at 10:00 and service returns at 10:45. The RTO is 30 minutes. By how many minutes was it missed?
hints: Work out the length of the outage in minutes.
The outage was 45 minutes.
Subtract the allowed time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The outage lasted 45 minutes against 30 allowed, so it was missed by 15 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: Missing an RTO has a cost; the point of stating it in advance is to design the recovery to fit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the outage length. The question asks for the excess.
That is the objective, not the excess.

questions.prompt: Which feature exists mainly to survive an availability-zone failure?
hints: Which one sits in a different zone and takes over automatically?
Replicas, caches and larger instances serve other goals.
questions.onCorrect: A synchronous standby in another zone means a failover loses no committed data.

misconceptions.feedback: A replica scales reads and lags behind; it is not meant to take over as a primary.
More capacity in one zone is still in one zone.
A cache speeds up reads and does not hold the data safely.

questions.prompt: Which kind of scaling has a hard ceiling, the size of the largest machine, and leaves a single point of failure: scaling up or scaling out?
hints: One of the two keeps a single machine.
The other adds more machines.
questions.onCorrect: Scaling out removes both limits, which is why it is the usual answer for a service that has to keep growing.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding machines has no single-machine ceiling, and one failure costs only a share.

questions.prompt: Messages arrive at 120 a second, and two workers handle 50 a second each. What happens to the backlog of waiting messages?
hints: Compare what the two workers finish each second with what arrives.

acceptedIdeas: It grows for as long as the load lasts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It grows for as long as the load lasts

questions.onCorrect: Whenever arrivals exceed capacity the backlog grows, and it keeps growing for as long as that holds.

choices.label: It grows for as long as the load lasts

misconceptions.feedback: The two workers finish 100 a second between them, so 20 more arrive each second than leave, and the difference accumulates.
Shrinking needs the workers to finish more than arrives, and here they finish 100 a second against 120 arriving.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: 260 messages arrive each second and one worker handles 60 a second. What is the least whole number of workers that keeps up?
hints: Divide the arrival rate by one worker's rate.
The quotient is about 4.33.
Workers come in whole numbers, and a fraction means another is needed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 260 ÷ 60 ≈ 4.33, and whole workers must cover that, so the answer is 5.

questions.onCorrect: Rounding up is not a courtesy: four workers would fall behind by 20 a second.

misconceptions.feedback: Four workers handle 240 a second, which falls short of 260.
A worker cannot be divided. Round up to a whole number.

questions.prompt: 150 messages arrive each second and one worker handles 40 a second. What is the least whole number of workers that keeps up?
hints: Divide the arrival rate by one worker's rate.
The quotient is 3.75.
Round up to a whole worker.
questions.onCorrect: Three workers handle 120 a second, which falls short, so a fourth is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Three workers handle 120 a second, which is below 150.
That is the exact quotient. Workers come in whole numbers.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: arrivals are 270 a second and 4 workers handle 240 a second in total. How many messages does the backlog gain in 5 minutes?
hints: Find the gap between arrivals and capacity each second.
The backlog gains 30 each second.
Multiply by the number of seconds in 5 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: The backlog is the integral of the gap, so a small shortfall still builds a large pile if it lasts.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gain each second. The question asks about 5 minutes.
That multiplies 240 by 300. The gain each second is the difference of the two rates.

questions.prompt: The queue holds 6,000 messages after a burst. Arrivals fall to 60 a second, and 2 workers handle 100 a second in total. How many seconds does the backlog take to empty?
hints: While workers are busy, the backlog falls by the gap between capacity and arrivals.
Capacity 100 against arrivals 60 gives a gap of 40 a second.
Divide the backlog by that gap.
questions.onCorrect: Draining is slower than it looks, because the system is still taking in new work while it clears the old.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the arrival rate. The backlog falls by the gap between capacity and arrivals.
That is the gap each second. Divide the backlog by it.

questions.prompt: 200 messages arrive each second and each worker handles 30 a second. What is the least whole number of workers that keeps up?
hints: Divide the arrival rate by one worker's rate.
The quotient is a little over six and a half.
Round up to a whole worker.
questions.onCorrect: Six workers handle 180 a second and the backlog would grow, so a seventh is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: Six workers handle 180 a second, which is below 200.
That is the exact quotient. Workers come in whole numbers.

questions.prompt: Arrivals are 150 a second and 4 workers handle 30 a second each. How many messages does the backlog gain in 10 minutes?
hints: Find the total capacity of the 4 workers.
Capacity is 120 a second, so arrivals exceed it by 30.
Ten minutes is 600 seconds; multiply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 × 30 = 120 a second of capacity, so the gain is 150 − 120 = 30 a second, and 30 × 600 = 18,000.

questions.onCorrect: A backlog of this size takes minutes to clear even once capacity is restored.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gain each second. Multiply by the number of seconds.
That uses 100 seconds. Ten minutes is 600 seconds.

questions.prompt: What must a tier be for any instance behind a load balancer to be able to serve any request?
hints: Think about where a user's data lives between requests.
Any instance serving any request means no instance holds what the others lack.
questions.onCorrect: A stateless tier keeps its per-user data in a shared store, so instances can be added or removed freely.

misconceptions.feedback: A stateful tier holds user data locally, which ties users to one instance.
Threading is about how one instance runs its work, not which instance serves a request.
Encryption protects data and has no bearing on which instance can serve a request.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: 650 GB is stored at $0.023 per GB-month. What is the monthly cost in dollars?
hints: Cost is the amount stored times the price per gigabyte.
Multiply 650 by 0.023.
Give the answer in dollars with cents.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026. Storage is usually the smallest line on a bill like this one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price per gigabyte. Multiply by the 650 gigabytes.
Check the decimal point: 650 × 0.023 is not 149.5.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: 1,500 GB leaves the provider network at $0.09 per GB. What is the cost in dollars?
hints: Cost is the amount sent out times the price per gigabyte.
Multiply 1,500 by 0.09.
Data going in is usually free, so only what leaves counts.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026. Data going out is billed per gigabyte, and here it costs about nine times as much as storing the 650 GB.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price per gigabyte. Multiply by the number of gigabytes.
Check the decimal point: 1,500 × 0.09.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: the storage costs $14.95 and the data leaving costs $135.00. What is the total in dollars?
hints: Add the two lines of the bill.
Add the dollars and then the cents.
Give the answer with cents.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative prices, November 2026. A real bill has more lines, and each is worked out the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the storage. The total includes both lines.
That leaves out the data leaving. The total includes both lines.

questions.prompt: A team stops a virtual machine each night to save money. Which of its resources keeps being charged while the machine is stopped?
hints: Ask which resource still exists while the machine is off.
questions.onCorrect: The volume holds the data while the machine is off, so its charge continues until the volume is deleted.

choices.label: Neither, since a stopped machine costs nothing

misconceptions.feedback: Compute is billed for the hours a machine runs, so stopping it ends that charge.
Stopping ends the compute charge, but anything that goes on holding data for the machine is still billed by the GB-month.

questions.prompt: Finish the estimate: a virtual machine at $0.10 an hour runs 12 hours a day on 21 working days a month. What does it cost in a month, in dollars?
hints: Count the hours it actually runs.
Multiply the hours each day by the working days in the month.
Multiply those hours by $0.10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 × 21 = 252 hours, and 252 × 0.10 = 25.20, against 73.00 for a full month.

questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026. Switching off idle capacity is the clearest way elasticity saves money.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a full month of 730 hours. This machine runs only in working hours.
Check the number of hours run each month, which is far fewer than the hours in a month.

questions.prompt: Finish the working: a commitment with a 45% discount is paid for the whole month, used or not. At what percentage of the month in use does on demand cost the same?
hints: On demand costs the full price times the share of the month used.
The commitment costs a fixed amount whatever the use.
The two are equal when the share used equals the share paid.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The commitment costs 100% − 45% = 55% of the full price, and on demand costs 100% × u, so they are equal at u = 55%.

questions.onCorrect: Below that use the commitment wastes money, and above it the commitment saves.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the discount. The break-even is the share of the price still paid.
At full use the commitment is cheaper. The cost lines cross earlier.
That is the break-even for the 40% discount in the chart. Here the discount is 45%.

questions.prompt: A commitment gives a 30% discount and is paid for the whole month, used or not. At what percentage of the month in use does on demand cost the same?
hints: The commitment costs a fixed amount whatever the use.
On demand costs the full price times the share of the month used.
The two are equal when the share used equals the share paid.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The commitment costs 100% − 30% = 70% of the full price, and on demand costs 100% × u, so they are equal at u = 70%.

questions.onCorrect: A smaller discount raises the break-even, so the commitment pays off only for steadier loads.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the discount. The break-even is the share of the price still paid.
That is the figure for a 40% discount. A smaller discount shifts it up.

questions.prompt: 800 GB is stored at $0.023 per GB-month. What is the monthly cost in dollars?
hints: Multiply the amount stored by the price per gigabyte.
Give the answer in dollars with cents.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price for one gigabyte.
Check the decimal point.

questions.prompt: 3,500 GB leaves the provider network at $0.09 per GB. What is the cost in dollars?
hints: Multiply the amount sent out by the price per gigabyte.
Data entering is not charged.
questions.onCorrect: Illustrative price, November 2026. Serving large files to users is where this line grows quickly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price per gigabyte.
Check the decimal point.

questions.prompt: A team stops a virtual machine to save money. Which charge continues?
hints: Stopping ends the running hours.
Something the machine owned is still allocated.
questions.onCorrect: Orphaned volumes are a common surprise: unattached ones keep billing until someone deletes them.

misconceptions.feedback: Compute is billed for the hours the machine runs, and a stopped machine does not run.
Data transfer in is usually free in any case.
The disk is still allocated, so it still costs.

questions.prompt: Which pillar covers protecting information and systems, for example by granting only the access a task needs?
hints: It is the pillar the IAM lesson belonged to.
Think of identity, encryption and detection.
questions.onCorrect: Security is one of the six pillars, and it also runs through the others, since a reliable design that leaks data is not a good one.

misconceptions.feedback: Reliability is about recovering from failure. Protecting data and limiting access is a different pillar.
