questions.prompt: Adding a second region raises a design's reliability. Which pillar usually pays for the improvement?
hints: Ask what a second region doubles.
questions.onCorrect: A second region doubles much of the running estate and adds the work of keeping the regions in step.

misconceptions.feedback: A second region need not weaken security, but it does double much of what is running and has to be paid for.
Performance is usually unchanged, or better for users near the second region, while the running estate roughly doubles.

questions.prompt: Finish the review: which pillar does spreading the servers across two zones mainly serve?
hints: Ask what the design survives that it would not survive in one zone.
The loss of a zone is a failure.
questions.onCorrect: Surviving the loss of a zone is the clearest example of a reliability choice.

misconceptions.feedback: Zones do not change who may access the system.
Two zones usually cost more, so the cost pillar is the one that pays, not the one served.

questions.prompt: Finish the review: which pillar does switching instances off outside working hours mainly serve?
hints: Ask what stops being charged when the instances are off.
Idle resources are a form of waste.
questions.onCorrect: It also helps sustainability, because machines that are off use no power, which shows that two pillars can pull the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: Switching things off does not make a system more reliable, and can even add risk. The saving falls on another pillar.

questions.prompt: A team proposes running a second region for an internal weekly report that can be rerun in an hour if it fails. Which assessment fits the Well-Architected view?
hints: Compare what the report needs with what a second region provides.
A trade-off has to be justified by what the workload needs.

acceptedIdeas: Question it: the reliability gained is small against the cost and complexity added
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Question it: the reliability gained is small against the cost and complexity added

questions.onCorrect: The workload's goals decide, and a rerunnable weekly report has a very loose recovery need.

choices.label: Approve it: reliability should always be at its maximum
Approve it: more regions always improve every pillar
Reject it: a second region is never worth the price
Question it: the reliability gained is small against the cost and complexity added

misconceptions.feedback: Maximum reliability is not a goal in itself; it is bought with other pillars.
Some workloads do justify a second region. It is a question of need, not a ban.
A second region raises reliability and lowers cost and simplicity. It does not improve every pillar.

questions.prompt: How many pillars does the current AWS Well-Architected Framework have?
hints: Operational excellence, security and reliability are the first three.
Performance efficiency and cost optimisation are the next two.
One more was added in 2021.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pillars are operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability: six.

questions.onCorrect: Sustainability was added as a sixth pillar in 2021.

misconceptions.feedback: Five pillars was the number before sustainability was added in 2021.
Three is the number of service models in the first lesson. There are more pillars than that.

questions.prompt: Adding a second region mainly raises which pillar, and costs which?
hints: A second region is a second copy of the estate.
What does a second copy protect against, and what does it add to the bill?
questions.onCorrect: Every pillar choice has a counterpart; recording it is the point of a review.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the direction: more regions add expense, and what they buy is protection from failure.
A second region does not trade performance for security.
A second region does not weaken reliability.

questions.prompt: Which pillar covers running and monitoring systems and improving procedures?
hints: It is the pillar about how the work is done day to day.
The first pillar in the list.
questions.onCorrect: Its design principles include performing operations as code and learning from failures.

misconceptions.feedback: Reliability is about recovering from failures. Running and improving procedures is the first pillar.

questions.prompt: The data in a bucket is encrypted, yet anyone on the internet can read it. Name the S3 setting that stops public access at the bucket or account level.
hints: Encryption does not decide who may read; something else does.
The setting has the word public in its name.
questions.onCorrect: Block Public Access overrides policies that would otherwise grant access to everyone.

misconceptions.feedback: Encryption protects the bytes at rest, but the service decrypts them for anyone the policy lets in.

questions.prompt: A bucket was made public last week, and its owner wants to know which principal changed its policy, and when. Which kind of record would show that?
hints: You need a history of actions, with who took each one.

acceptedIdeas: An audit log of the calls made in the account
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An audit log of the calls made in the account

questions.onCorrect: Provider audit logs record every API call, including the ones that changed the bucket.

choices.label: An audit log of the calls made in the account
The settings of the bucket's encryption key
The bucket's access policy as it stands now

misconceptions.feedback: The current policy shows what is allowed now, but not who changed it or when.
Encryption settings say how the data is protected at rest, and they keep no history of who changed a bucket policy.

questions.prompt: Finish the reading: the event has the error code AccessDenied. Did the policy change take effect? Answer yes or no.
hints: An error code appears only when something went wrong.
The call was refused.
questions.onCorrect: Failed attempts are logged too, which is useful: a run of denials can show someone probing.

misconceptions.feedback: An AccessDenied code means the call was refused, and the setting stayed as it was.

questions.prompt: Finish the reading: a log excerpt holds 8 events, and 3 of them carry the error code AccessDenied. How many succeeded?
hints: An event with an error code failed.
Work out how many events have no error code.
Subtract the failed ones from the total.
questions.onCorrect: Eight events, three refused: the five without an error succeeded, and those are the ones to check.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number that failed. The question asks how many succeeded.
That is every event. Some of them failed.

questions.prompt: A company splits 10 equal workloads evenly across 5 accounts, and one account is compromised. How much of the company's work is exposed?
hints: Ask what an account separates from the others.
Count the workloads inside one account.

acceptedIdeas: The 2 workloads in that account, a fifth of the total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 2 workloads in that account, a fifth of the total

questions.onCorrect: In one account all 10 would be exposed: separation limits what a single mistake or attacker can reach.

choices.label: Half of them, the workloads that share its region
The 2 workloads in that account, a fifth of the total
All 10, since the accounts belong to one organisation

misconceptions.feedback: An account is an isolation boundary, so credentials and resources in one do not reach into the others by default.
Regions do not decide the exposure here, because the account is the boundary and only the workloads inside it are reachable.

questions.prompt: A company wants to stop everyone in every account, administrators included, from switching off audit logging. Which kind of organisation-wide policy sets this limit, as a maximum on the permissions of the accounts under it, without granting any access itself? Use its full name or its initials.
hints: It is attached to the organisation, a unit or an account.
It acts as a filter on what IAM policies can grant.
questions.onCorrect: Service control policies bound what any principal in an account can do, even an administrator, without giving anyone access on their own.

misconceptions.feedback: An IAM policy grants access to a principal. The one asked about sets an upper bound over many accounts.

questions.prompt: A bucket is encrypted but readable by anyone on the internet. Which control actually fixes the exposure?
hints: Encryption protects stored bytes; it does not decide who may ask for them.
Which option changes who is allowed to read?

acceptedIdeas: Block public access, or a tighter access policy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Block public access, or a tighter access policy

questions.onCorrect: Encryption and access control are separate layers, and a service decrypts for anyone the policy admits.

choices.label: Block public access, or a tighter access policy

misconceptions.feedback: The data is already encrypted. The exposure comes from who is allowed to read it.
The size of the bucket has no bearing on who can read it.
A second region adds another copy, and could copy the same exposure.

questions.prompt: Which kind of log records who called which provider API and when?
hints: It records calls to the provider's own interface.
Think of who, what, when and from where.
questions.onCorrect: In AWS this role is filled by CloudTrail, which records API calls from the console, the command line and code alike.

misconceptions.feedback: Those record traffic to resources. The log asked about records calls that manage them.

questions.prompt: Why use separate accounts for production and development?
hints: Think about what one mistake or one stolen credential can reach.
An account is a boundary that policies do not cross unless you allow it.

acceptedIdeas: To limit the blast radius of mistakes and compromise
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To limit the blast radius of mistakes and compromise

questions.onCorrect: An account is the strongest isolation boundary a provider offers, so trouble in one stays there.

choices.label: To limit the blast radius of mistakes and compromise
It removes the need for IAM

misconceptions.feedback: Separate accounts do not lower the bill; they sometimes add small overheads.
Accounts have no effect on network speed.
Each account still needs IAM. Separation adds a boundary and does not replace it.

questions.prompt: Which recovery strategy keeps only core data and minimal infrastructure running, and scales up when a disaster strikes?
hints: It sits between keeping backups only and running a small full copy.
Think of the small flame that can light a whole boiler.
questions.onCorrect: The core of the system is already running, which shortens the recovery compared with rebuilding from backups.

misconceptions.feedback: Backups alone keep nothing running. The strategy asked about keeps a core alive.
A warm standby runs a whole scaled-down copy, which is more than the minimum.

questions.prompt: A web tier needs 4 servers to carry its peak load. It is spread over two availability zones and must keep serving at peak if either zone is lost. Roughly how many servers does it run in total?
hints: Ask what is left running after one zone is lost.

acceptedIdeas: 8, enough for the full peak in each zone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 8, enough for the full peak in each zone

questions.onCorrect: Surviving the loss of a zone this way means paying for the peak twice over.

choices.label: About 6, with a little spare in each zone
8, enough for the full peak in each zone

misconceptions.feedback: If one zone is lost, the two servers in the other zone are left to carry a load that needs 4.
After a zone is lost only the servers in the other zone remain, and they must carry the whole peak on their own.

questions.prompt: Finish the choice: the requirement is an RTO of 10 minutes and an RPO of 1 minute, and traffic need not be served from two regions at once. Which strategy fits: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby or active/active?
hints: The recovery must happen in minutes, which rules out the two cheapest strategies.
Running both regions at full load is more than the target needs.
questions.onCorrect: A scaled-down full system can be scaled up in minutes, without paying for a second fully loaded region.

misconceptions.feedback: Active/active would meet the target, but it costs the most and the target does not require near-zero recovery.
Starting servers from cold takes longer than the tens of minutes this strategy usually needs.

questions.prompt: Finish the choice: the requirement is an RTO of 24 hours and an RPO of 12 hours, with a very small budget. Which strategy is enough?
hints: Both targets are measured in hours, not minutes.
The cheapest strategy keeps no second system running.
questions.onCorrect: Looser targets justify the cheapest strategy; paying for more would buy recovery speed nobody asked for.

misconceptions.feedback: That would work but costs more than the targets need. The cheapest strategy keeps only copies of the data.

questions.prompt: A web tier needs 8 servers at peak and must survive the loss of any one of 3 zones. The servers are spread evenly, and the two remaining zones must still carry the full peak. How many servers run in total?
hints: After one zone is lost, two zones remain.
Each remaining zone must carry half of 8, which is 4 servers.
Every one of the 3 zones needs that many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two zones must carry 8 servers, so each runs 4, and 3 × 4 = 12 servers run in total.

questions.onCorrect: Spreading over more zones makes each zone smaller, so the extra capacity for failure falls from 100% to 50%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the peak itself. The spare capacity for a lost zone is extra.
That is the figure for two zones, each carrying the full peak.

questions.prompt: A web tier needs 12 servers at peak and must survive the loss of any one of 4 zones, with the servers spread evenly. How many servers run in total?
hints: After one zone is lost, the other zones must still carry the peak.
Three zones carry the peak, so each carries a third of it.
Every one of the zones needs that many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three zones carry 12, so each runs 4, and 4 × 4 = 16 servers run in total.

questions.onCorrect: More zones make the cost of surviving one failure smaller, up to the point where the added complexity outweighs it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the peak. Extra capacity is needed for the lost zone.
That is the figure for two zones, each able to carry the full peak.

questions.prompt: Which strategy keeps only core data and minimal infrastructure running, scaling up at disaster time?
hints: It keeps something running, but not a whole system.
It is more than backups and less than a scaled-down copy.
questions.onCorrect: A pilot light starts the rest of the estate around a core that is already alive.

misconceptions.feedback: Backups keep nothing running, so everything has to be built at disaster time.
A warm standby runs a complete system at reduced size, which is more than the minimum.
Active/active runs a full copy that serves users, the opposite of minimal.

questions.prompt: Which strategy has the shortest recovery time and the highest cost?
hints: Recovery gets faster as more of the system is already running.
Which strategy has all of it running all the time?
questions.onCorrect: Because both regions already serve traffic, a regional failure is mostly a matter of rerouting.

misconceptions.feedback: That has the longest recovery time and the lowest cost.
That is faster than backups and slower than a standby, at a middle cost.
That is fast and costly, but the strategy that keeps a full copy serving traffic is faster and costlier.

questions.prompt: A two-zone web tier runs 5 servers per zone, and each zone alone must carry the full peak load. How many servers are needed in total?
hints: Each zone must be able to carry the full peak.
A zone does that with 5 servers.
Add the two zones together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each zone runs 5 servers, so 2 × 5 = 10 in total.

questions.onCorrect: The cost of surviving a zone loss with two zones is a doubling of the web tier.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one zone. The other zone needs as many.
That is the number of zones. Each runs several servers.

questions.prompt: A build server's job needs s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on 4 named buckets, which is 8 action-and-bucket pairs. A proposed policy lets it call 12 listed S3 actions on the same 4 buckets. How does the proposal measure against least privilege?
hints: Pairs multiply: actions times buckets.
Compare the pairs granted with the pairs the job uses.

acceptedIdeas: It grants 48 pairs where the job needs 8, so the extra 40 should be removed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It grants 48 pairs where the job needs 8, so the extra 40 should be removed

questions.onCorrect: Each unneeded pair is something a leaked credential or a bug could do that the job never needed, so narrower grants shrink what can go wrong.

choices.label: It meets least privilege, since it lists actions instead of using s3:*
It grants 48 pairs where the job needs 8, so the extra 40 should be removed
It meets least privilege, since it still names only 4 buckets
It grants 16 pairs, twice what the job needs

misconceptions.feedback: Naming the buckets limits the resources, but least privilege limits the actions too, and ten of the twelve are ones the job never calls.
Listing actions by name is narrower than s3:*, yet the list still holds ten actions the job never uses.
Each of the 12 actions applies to each of the 4 buckets, so the pairs are found by multiplying the two counts, not by doubling the pairs the job uses.

flashcards.front: Name the service model where the customer manages the OS, runtime, application and data.
flashcards.back: IaaS: the provider runs facility, hardware and hypervisor, and the customer runs everything above them.

flashcards.front: Who patches the guest OS of a virtual machine you rent, the provider or the customer?
flashcards.back: The customer, because under IaaS the operating system inside the machine is yours.

flashcards.front: Explain why moving to the cloud does not make security the provider's problem.
flashcards.back: The provider secures the cloud itself, while configuration and data stay with the customer.

flashcards.front: Components with 99.9% availability each, two in series and independent: availability as a percentage?
Name the unit of isolation inside a region, one or more discrete data centres.
flashcards.back: An availability zone: one or more discrete data centres with their own power, networking and cooling.

flashcards.front: Explain why two servers in one zone do not give high availability.
flashcards.back: A zone failure removes both servers together, so the failures are not independent.

flashcards.front: What decision does a request get if no policy allows it?
flashcards.back: Denied by default, because access has to be granted.

flashcards.front: Name an IAM identity assumed temporarily, with short-lived credentials.
flashcards.back: A role: assumed credentials expire, so there is no long-lived key to steal.

flashcards.front: Explain why an explicit deny always beats an allow.
flashcards.back: Evaluation checks for explicit denies first, so a deny in any policy ends the evaluation.

flashcards.front: How many addresses in a /28?
flashcards.back: 2^(32−28) = 16 addresses, and 11 are usable on AWS.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^(32−28) = 16 addresses, and 11 are usable on AWS.

flashcards.front: Which filter is stateful and attached to a resource: security group or network ACL?
flashcards.back: A security group: it remembers connections, so replies are allowed without a second rule.

flashcards.front: Explain what makes a subnet public rather than private.
flashcards.back: Its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway, and its resources have public addresses.

flashcards.front: Name the compute model that runs code per event, billed by requests and duration.
flashcards.back: A function (function as a service): no server to manage, and idle time costs nothing.

flashcards.front: Three instances at $0.10 an hour over 730 hours: monthly cost in dollars?
flashcards.back: 0.10 × 730 × 3 = 219.00 (illustrative price).

flashcards.front: Explain why serverless does not mean there are no servers.
flashcards.back: Servers still run the code, and the provider manages them so the customer does not.

flashcards.front: Which storage kind is a raw disk attached to one machine?
flashcards.back: Block storage: an operating system or database engine reads and writes it as a disk.

flashcards.front: Annual loss chance per object 10^-11; expected losses among 10^8 objects? (decimal)
Explain why replicating a bucket does not replace a backup.
flashcards.back: Replication copies deletions and corruption as faithfully as good data, so earlier versions need separate protection.

flashcards.front: Backups every 4 hours: worst-case RPO in hours?
flashcards.back: The worst case is a failure just before the next backup: 4 hours.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The worst case is a failure just before the next backup: 4 hours.

flashcards.front: Which has the job of failover: a multi-AZ standby or a read replica?
flashcards.back: The multi-AZ standby, which is kept in step synchronously in another zone.

flashcards.front: Explain what RPO and RTO each measure.
flashcards.back: RPO is the most data, as time, you can afford to lose; RTO is the longest outage you can afford.

flashcards.front: 120 arrive a second; each worker handles 50. Least whole number of workers?
flashcards.back: 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4, which rounds up to 3.

flashcards.front: Name the property of a tier that lets any instance serve any request.
flashcards.back: Stateless: per-user data lives in a shared store, not in the instance.

flashcards.front: Explain why a queue hides a slow consumer instead of curing it.
flashcards.back: The queue absorbs the excess, but if arrivals stay above capacity the backlog grows without bound.

flashcards.front: 2,000 GB out at $0.09 per GB: cost in dollars?
flashcards.back: 2,000 × 0.09 = 180.00 (illustrative price).

flashcards.front: Name the kind of data transfer that providers usually charge for per GB.
flashcards.back: Data going out of the provider network, or across regions; data coming in is usually free.

flashcards.front: Explain why a commitment saves money only above a break-even level of use.
flashcards.back: You pay the committed price whether you use the capacity or not, so unused hours waste it.

flashcards.front: How many pillars does the AWS Well-Architected Framework have?
flashcards.back: Six: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability.

flashcards.front: Name the pillar added to the AWS Well-Architected Framework in 2021.
flashcards.back: Sustainability, which covers reducing the environmental impact of running workloads.

flashcards.front: Explain why a design should record the trade-off behind each choice.
flashcards.back: Strengthening one pillar usually costs another, and a recorded trade-off lets a later reviewer see whether it still holds.

flashcards.front: Name the log that records who called which provider API, and when.
flashcards.back: The audit log (AWS CloudTrail): who, what, when and from where, for every API call.

flashcards.front: Name the policy type that caps what accounts in an organisation may do without granting any access.
flashcards.back: A service control policy, which is a guardrail over many accounts.

flashcards.front: Explain why encrypting a bucket does not make a public bucket safe.
flashcards.back: Encryption protects the bytes at rest, but the service decrypts them for anyone the access policy admits.

flashcards.front: Name the recovery strategy that runs a scaled-down but complete system in the second region.
flashcards.back: Warm standby: a small full copy that can be scaled up to take over.

flashcards.front: Name the recovery strategy with the fastest recovery and the highest cost.
flashcards.back: Multi-site active/active: both regions serve users all the time.

flashcards.front: Explain why a backup that has never been restored is only a hope.
flashcards.back: An untested restore can fail for reasons nobody has met yet, and restoring from nothing takes the longest.
